items.title: “We Love Our Tops and Bottoms”: The 25 Wildest Quotes From Grindr CEO George Arison’s AMA
items.author: Clapback
items.content:
George Arison took Grindr’s earnings story to r/wallstreetbets. Reddit responded with memes, pointed questions, and the occasional surprisingly candid answer.

On November 6, [Grindr CEO George Arison hosted an ask-me-anything session](https://www.reddit.com/r/wallstreetbets/comments/1xpgjl2/im_george_arison_ceo_of_grindr_grnd_we_reported/ .) in r/wallstreetbets after the company reported third-quarter results. He came to discuss the publicly traded company’s future as a consumer AI platform, its nearly 16 million monthly users, and its expansion into healthcare. The subreddit had other ideas.

The thread mixed earnest questions about privacy and ads with relentless innuendo about stock-market “bears,” fast-food dumpsters, and the company’s name. Below are 25 of the most memorable exchanges and comments, with Arison’s responses identified separately from Reddit jokes and unverified allegations.

The bluntest question was also among the thread’s most popular. It set the tone for a Q&A where no corporate talking point was safe. It was the most direct possible collision between a corporate earnings tour and Reddit culture. The question became a referendum on whether a CEO could survive a forum that treats every setup as an invitation to meme. Arison did not answer this particular one in the supplied transcript.

2. “This is where the magic happens.”

Asked why he chose wallstreetbets rather than a more conventional community, Arison supplied the most concise possible defense of the venue. That four-word reply is arguably the clearest evidence that Arison understood the assignment. WallStreetBets is not an obvious investor-relations venue for a dating platform; it is a place where a ticker symbol and a punchline can become the same thing. Rather than apologize for the choice, he embraced the chaos.

3. “Grindr does not crash ;)”

A user asked about supposed outages during Republican National Conventions. Arison’s playful denial did not establish anything about traffic at political events. The joke leaned on recurring internet rumors about spikes in Grindr use during Republican political gatherings. His wink turned a loaded question into a brand moment, but it should not be mistaken for independent evidence about usage at conventions. The distinction matters: the question was a joke, the answer was a denial.

4. “We love our tops and bottoms”

A question about top-line versus bottom-line growth earned a reply that was both on-brand and almost completely devoid of financial guidance. This was a genuine question about financial performance disguised as a perfect double entendre. Arison answered with a line engineered for screenshots. For investors looking for margin guidance, it offered precisely zero basis points of insight; for everyone else, it was the AMA’s most shareable earnings commentary.

5. “I’ve actually never eaten at Wendy’s”

A wallstreetbets question invoked the subreddit’s favorite fast-food chain and its dumpster lore. Arison took the bait, then pivoted to inflation. Wendy’s is a recurring landmark in WallStreetBets humor, where failed trades are imagined ending behind the restaurant’s dumpster. Arison’s confession that he had never eaten there briefly made the CEO sound like a tourist visiting Reddit’s national monument. Then he did something stranger: he answered the economics part seriously.

6. “But no, $20 is not $20.”

Arison turned a crude running joke into a surprisingly serious comment about affordability and housing access. In the same reply, Arison moved from a $20 joke to housing affordability. It was a whiplash-inducing pivot from meme economics to actual economics, and one of the rare moments when the CEO sounded less like a corporate spokesperson than a person with a view on public policy.

7. “I paid for premium membership for 2 years without realizing it. I’m not even gay”

The commenter asked for a refund. No CEO answer appears in the supplied thread excerpt. The commenter claimed to have paid for a subscription for two years without using the service, then asked whether a refund was still possible. It is an absurd customer-support ticket to bring to an earnings AMA, but it also highlights the awkwardness of subscription businesses: revenue can keep arriving long after a customer stops paying attention. No refund decision was shown.

8. “Grindr has an exposed backend”

The pun appeared beneath a commenter’s allegation about a past security interview and subsequent breach. The underlying allegation is not verified by the AMA transcript. The pun followed a far more serious, unverified allegation about a security interview and a subsequent data incident. Reddit immediately converted the phrase “exposed backend” into innuendo. That tonal switch captures the entire thread: potentially consequential privacy questions competing with the urge to make the next joke.

Behind the jokes was a consequential challenge about protecting sensitive user data. The supplied excerpt does not show Arison answering this specific question. This was one of the AMA’s strongest questions because Grindr handles information that can be unusually sensitive. The commenter described a personal interview experience and alleged a later breach; those claims should not be treated as established facts without separate reporting. The question itself remains important, and the provided excerpt contains no direct answer to it.

10. “We maintain an internal ‘dangerous neighborhoods’ list”

In a separate security answer, Arison described safeguards in higher-risk countries, including hiding distance, blocking screenshots of certain media, and removing third-party ads. Arison’s detailed response to another user gave a rare look at how the company says it adapts product features to legal and physical risks. Turning off distance and discovery features, restricting screenshots, and removing third-party advertising are concrete design choices, not just a promise to take privacy seriously. The safeguards are the company’s description and deserve independent scrutiny.

11. “Gay people are like everyone else.”

Asked whether gay people like AI, Arison pushed back on the premise before suggesting gay men often adopt new technology early. Asked whether gay people like AI, Arison rejected the idea that a diverse community shares one view. He then offered a more provocative business thesis: gay men have historically been early technology adopters. His iPhone anecdote was presented as an analysis he had encountered, not as a verified figure in the AMA.

12. “People produce about 50+ messages a day on average”

The CEO’s engagement claim helped explain why he describes Grindr as an open social network rather than a swipe-to-match dating app. The claim is one of the most consequential numbers in the discussion. If an average user sends more than 50 messages daily, Grindr is selling investors engagement and network effects, not simply swipes or dates. It also helps explain why the company wants to add services around existing conversations rather than build a separate audience from scratch.

13. “We are more of a social network for gay people vs. a dating product”

This distinction was the backbone of his business pitch: expand from dating into travel, community, AI services, and healthcare. This is the strategic repositioning behind the jokes. Dating apps are often judged on matching and churn; social networks are judged on ongoing utility, identity, and community. Arison wants Grindr in the second category, which would justify building adjacent products even after a user finds a partner.

14. “Grindr ‘was about sex.’”

Arison said a large financial firm had declined to work with Grindr for that reason, and called the attitude fundamentally homophobic. This is his account of the exchange. Arison said a large financial firm once declined to work with Grindr because it was “about sex,” a rationale he characterized as homophobic. The story reframes a commercial objection as a question of whether gay-focused products are treated differently from mainstream dating businesses. The firm was not named in the AMA.

15. “We are responsible for a quarter of gay relationships in the United States.”

A striking company claim emerged in an answer about why successful relationships need not hurt retention. A quarter of gay relationships is an enormous claim about cultural reach, and it came in response to a question about whether successful relationships hurt retention. Arison’s argument was that couples can still use Grindr for friends, travel, and community. The percentage is his claim; the transcript does not provide the underlying study.

The strongest conventional management advice in the thread: choose two to four priorities instead of trying to do everything. This is probably the most reusable management advice in the entire exchange. His point was not that ideas are scarce, but that attention is. The CEO said he tries to identify two to four priorities at a time and refuse distractions, a surprisingly disciplined philosophy in an AMA overflowing with them.

17. “I’ve become much more of a Reddit user recently because so much of the content you get from AI is from Reddit”

An unexpected explanation of why the CEO has been spending more time on the platform. There is a wonderfully recursive quality to this answer: an AI-focused CEO goes to Reddit partly because AI draws from Reddit. It also hints at a distribution shift. Forums are not just communities to speak to; they are increasingly part of the text ecosystem that shapes how people encounter information through AI products.

18. “This has been far more serious than I expected!”

Despite the chaos, Arison said the AMA contained more substantive discussion than he anticipated. It is hard to imagine what a CEO expects from WallStreetBets when introducing a publicly traded app whose name practically writes its own jokes. Yet Arison said the discussion was more serious than anticipated. That may be the strongest compliment the forum received all afternoon.

19. “One of the things that makes that possible is ads”

Responding to complaints about intrusive ads, Arison argued advertising helps keep Grindr free for 93% of users, while acknowledging the ad experience needs work. The advertising exchange exposed a real tension in the business. Arison defended ads as the mechanism that keeps the product free for most users while acknowledging the challenge of attracting direct advertisers. Users complaining about intrusive ads and a CEO defending free access can both be describing the same trade-off.

20. “My husband is an public health doctor who spent decades working on HIV”

Arison connected Grindr’s health ambitions to his family and to the company’s acquisition of telehealth provider Freddie. The Freddie acquisition was more than a growth talking point for Arison. He connected Grindr’s HIV-prevention ambitions to his husband’s long career in public health. That personal link gives the healthcare expansion an unusually human motivation, even as it remains a commercial initiative requiring execution.

21. “The Global Gayborhood”

The company’s aspirational phrase for a platform that encompasses more than dating, including an AI-powered premium tier and healthcare. “Global Gayborhood” sounds like branding, but it is also an acquisition strategy in two words. Grindr wants to be the starting point for multiple services serving gay men, with AI premium features and HIV-prevention healthcare as early examples. The challenge is expanding without eroding trust in the core app.

22. “I knew I was gay pretty early”

In one of the more personal answers, Arison described growing up in Soviet Georgia, coming out, and building a family with his husband. The most personal answer of the AMA traced Arison’s childhood in Soviet Georgia, where he said being openly gay did not feel possible, to his life as a husband and father. In a thread full of jokes about whether he uses the product, it was a reminder that his relationship with the company’s mission is not merely financial.

23. “Do you have a team reviewing each of your responses, or are you just raw dogging this”

Perhaps the perfect summary of the tension between a polished public-company AMA and the language of wallstreetbets. A surprisingly fair question, buried inside a phrase no corporate communications team would put in a briefing document. The AMA excerpt does not show an answer, so readers are left to judge the tone of the responses for themselves. The very fact that a CEO entertained this forum made the question inevitable.

Grindr trades under GRND. Showing up on the subreddit best known for retail-trading frenzies made the question inevitable. For a community obsessed with stocks becoming memes, the possibility that Grindr had deliberately wandered into meme-stock territory was too good to ignore. The question captures the risk of this kind of investor outreach: attention is easy to generate, but impossible to control once the comments take over.

25. “Can it flirt in rust?”

The user asked whether Grindr Edge was Claude-powered, then delivered a programming-language punchline. The excerpt includes no answer. The final joke combines the company’s AI push with a programming-language punchline. It is also a neat summary of the gap between a product roadmap and internet reception. Management wants to discuss AI-powered recommendations and premium features; Reddit wants to know whether the chatbot can flirt in Rust.

A meme thread with a real business underneath

The joke density was enormous, but the serious topics were substantial: how Grindr handles sensitive data, whether advertising has damaged the free experience, what AI will actually do for users, and whether healthcare can become a meaningful second business. Arison answered some of those questions directly and left others unanswered in the excerpt. The final joke combines the company’s AI push with a programming-language punchline. It is also a neat summary of the gap between a product roadmap and internet reception. Management wants to discuss AI-powered recommendations and premium features; Reddit wants to know whether the chatbot can flirt in Rust.

The broader lesson for tech executives considering an AMA: you can choose the talking points, but you cannot choose the questions. Arison seemed willing to play along, and the result was a rare earnings-adjacent conversation that was as much internet culture as investor relations. The final joke combines the company’s AI push with a programming-language punchline. It is also a neat summary of the gap between a product roadmap and internet reception. Management wants to discuss AI-powered recommendations and premium features; Reddit wants to know whether the chatbot can flirt in Rust.

items.title: Load Balancing Starts Before the Load Balancer: Routing Patterns for Distributed Systems
items.author: Varsha Ganesh
items.content:
This is the third in my series on control plane architecture and design patterns. See the first article on a high-level overview of control planes , and the second on the scaling component .

I ended my last piece on scaling with a promise to come back to hot partitions, i.e., the situation where a single piece of your system is hit with disproportionate traffic no matter how well the rest of your infrastructure is provisioned. That problem lives squarely in load balancing and routing, which is what I want to dig into here.

The thing that surprised me most when I actually started building these systems is how little "load balancing" has to do with load balancers, once you get past the simplest cases. A load balancer is one tool for solving a routing problem. It's not the only one, and for a lot of distributed systems, it's not even the primary one.

The Simple Case: Fronting Stateless Services

For a basic web application, load balancing is close to what most people picture:

  • DNS-based load balancing -  multiple A records pointing to different IPs, with clients or resolvers distributing requests across them. It's cheap and simple, but coarse: you get little control over how traffic is actually distributed, and DNS on its own has no real-time awareness of backend health. Many DNS providers let you associate health checks with your records so that unhealthy IPs get pulled out of rotation, which closes part of that gap. But those checks aren't free: each one is a probe you pay for and have to tune, and the cost grows with the number of endpoints and the frequency you check them. They also have no global view of the system. A check can tell you whether an endpoint responds, but not how loaded it is, how it compares to its peers, or whether pulling it out of rotation will overload the ones that remain.
  • A dedicated load balancer or proxy (an ALB, an NLB, nginx, Envoy) sitting in front of your fleet, actively health-checking backends and routing each connection or request according to an algorithm, e.g., round robin, least connections, weighted, or latency-based.

For stateless, interchangeable backends, this gets you most of the way there. Any healthy instance can serve any request, so the algorithm mostly just needs to avoid overloading any single one.

This is also where most teams' mental model of "load balancing" stops. It's worth pushing past that, because the moment your backend isn't stateless and interchangeable, this model stops being sufficient.

The Harder Case: Routing With State

A distributed database doesn't have interchangeable backends. Each host owns specific partitions of data, and a request for a given key has to go to the host that actually holds it (or a replica of it). You can't round-robin your way out of that.  The routing decision is now coupled to , which is a placement problem, not a traffic-distribution problem.

This is where load balancing stops being about the request path and starts being about the partitioning and placement strategy decided when data is written, long before any request shows up.

Placement Strategy Is Load Balancing in Advance

When a new table or dataset is created in a system like Cassandra, the control plane decides how its partitions get distributed and replicated across the fleet. Get that placement strategy wrong, and no amount of clever request routing fixes it later. You've already baked an imbalance into where the data lives.

Good placement strategies generally try to:

  • Spread partitions evenly across available hosts, so no single host owns a disproportionate share of the dataset
  • Respect replication and fault-domain constraints simultaneously - replicas of the same partition shouldn't land on the same rack or availability zone, even while you're optimizing for even distribution
  • Account for heterogeneous hardware; if your fleet isn't uniform, a host with double the capacity should reasonably get more partitions than one with less

None of this touches the request path directly. It's load balancing that happens at write time, and it's arguably the more important half of the problem.

The Problem Placement Alone Can't Solve: Hot Partitions

Even a well-designed placement strategy runs into a specific failure mode: hot partitions. This happens when traffic to specific keys is wildly uneven, usually because of a poorly chosen partition key (a timestamp, a low-cardinality value, a celebrity user ID) that concentrates requests onto one partition regardless of how evenly the was distributed.

The uncomfortable part is that this isn't something you can fully prevent through upfront design. Traffic patterns shift, applications evolve, and a key that was fine at launch can become a hotspot a year later. Detecting and correcting for it has to be an ongoing, automated function of the control plane, not a one-time decision.

  • Per-partition metrics, not just aggregate fleet metrics such as throughput, request count, and latency broken down at the partition level, since fleet-wide averages will hide a hot partition sitting next to a dozen idle ones
  • A threshold model that distinguishes a genuinely overloaded partition from normal variance. Naive fixed thresholds tend to either fire constantly on noisy workloads or miss slow-building hotspots
  • Attribution, ideally, knowing keys within a partition are driving the load helps decide whether splitting the partition will actually help, or whether the hot key will just follow you into the new split

Correcting for It: Re-Partitioning Live

Once a hot partition is identified, the fix is usually to split it and redistribute the pieces, but doing this against a partition serving live production traffic is one of the more delicate operations a control plane performs. A few things matter here:

  • The split has to be incremental and reversible. Splitting a partition in one atomic step against live traffic is asking for an outage; the operation needs to be able to pause, resume, or roll back mid-flight.
  • Routing has to update consistently with the split, so requests during the transition land on the correct new partition rather than the stale one. This usually means a routing/metadata layer that's updated as part of the same operation, not after it.
  • The new partitions need to actually solve the problem. If the hot key itself is the issue rather than uneven key distribution, splitting the partition just relocates the hotspot rather than resolving it. Sometimes the real fix is upstream, in how the application chooses partition keys in the first place.

Systems like DynamoDB build this kind of adaptive re-partitioning directly into their control plane, specifically so that a single misbehaving key doesn't require manual intervention every time it happens.

The Pattern Shows Up Everywhere Stateful Systems Do

Databases are the clearest illustration of placement-time routing, but the same problem, and largely the same solutions, show up anywhere a system shards state across a fleet. Two examples worth knowing well, because they each stress the pattern in a different direction.

A distributed cache like Redis Cluster or Memcached with consistent hashing looks superficially like the database case: keys are hashed to determine which shard owns them, and requests get routed accordingly. But caches diverge from databases in one important way that reshapes the whole routing problem - cache misses are cheap enough to tolerate, but hot keys are far more common and far more punishing.

Because caches sit in front of a slower system of record, a single viral key (a trending post, a flash-sale product, a piece of session data for a suddenly-popular event) can spike orders of magnitude above normal traffic in seconds, not the gradual drift you'd see with a hot database partition. A few things follow from that:

  • Consistent hashing helps with rebalancing, not hot keys. It minimizes how many keys move when you add or remove a shard, but it does nothing to stop one key from being disproportionately hot. The hash function doesn't know or care about request volume.
  • Client-side or edge-level request coalescing often matters more here than server-side re-sharding. If ten thousand requests for the same key arrive in the same second, the fix usually isn't "move this key to its own shard" (by the time you've detected and acted on it, the spike may already be over),  it's collapsing concurrent requests for the same key into one upstream fetch.
  • Local caching layers in front of the shard tier (an in-process cache on each application host, for instance) can absorb a hot-key spike before it ever reaches the sharded layer at all, which is often a simpler fix than trying to make the sharded routing layer reactive enough to keep up.

The routing decision for a cache miss is still a placement problem, i.e., determination of which shard owns this key. The operational fix for a hot key, however, usually lives one layer up from the routing logic itself, in how aggressively you can avoid sending duplicate requests downstream in the first place.

Systems like Kafka consumer groups or Flink jobs route by partition, much like a sharded database. A message with a given key is deterministically assigned to a partition, and a specific consumer or task instance owns that partition for processing.

But the load balancing constraint here is different in a way that matters: ordering guarantees typically require that all messages for a given key are processed by the same partition, in order, which means you can't rebalance a hot partition by simply splitting it the way you might with a database.

This creates a distinct set of routing trade-offs:

  • Partition count is usually a fixed, upfront decision. Unlike a database that can dynamically split an overloaded partition, most stream processing systems set partition count at topic-creation time, because increasing it later changes the key-to-partition mapping and can break ordering guarantees for existing consumers mid-stream. Getting this number right up front matters more here than almost anywhere else in the stack. Under-provision partitions and you have a hot-partition problem you architecturally cannot fix without a disruptive migration. Over-provisioning is the safer mistake, but it isn't free either: every partition carries its own log segments, file handles, and replication state on the brokers, so a very high count slows recovery after a broker failure (more partitions need new leaders), makes consumer group rebalances more disruptive, and shrinks producer batches, which hurts efficiency and latency. It also won't rescue you from a single hot key, since a given key always maps to one partition no matter how many exist. The practical target is enough headroom for foreseeable growth in consumer parallelism, not an arbitrarily large number "to be safe."
  • Consumer-side scaling is bounded by partition count, not by consumer group size. Adding more consumers than partitions doesn't help. The extra consumers just sit idle, so "scaling" a stream processing system often means capacity planning for partition count well ahead of actual load, rather than reactively adding resources the way you would with a stateless service.
  • Skewed key distribution is a design-time problem, not a runtime one. Because you can't cheaply reshuffle partitions after the fact, uneven key distribution (one customer ID generating 100x the events of any other) has to be addressed either in how keys are chosen, or by explicitly over-partitioning for the skew you expect by anticipating the hot path rather than reacting to it.

Stream processors push placement-time routing to its logical extreme: nearly all of the load balancing work happens at design time, because the ordering guarantees that make the system useful are exactly what make runtime rebalancing so constrained.

Load balancing in a distributed system operates on two timelines that are easy to conflate:

  • Request-time routing - the classic load balancer problem, distributing incoming requests across available, healthy backends
  • Placement-time routing - deciding, before any request arrives, where data or resources live in the first place, and continuously correcting that placement as traffic patterns change

For stateless services, the first one is basically the whole problem. For anything stateful and partitioned, the second one dominates, and it's a control plane responsibility that runs continuously in the background rather than a configuration you set once and forget.

Next in this series, I'll get into reliability guarantees - how control planes enforce promises (replication, TTL-based deletion, eventual consistency) that are genuinely hard to guarantee synchronously in the request path, and the auditing systems teams build to catch the gap between what a system promises and what it actually did.

items.title: Activists Breach Microsoft Data Center Construction Site As Protests Spread In Europe
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
More than 100 activists breached a Microsoft AI data center construction site in Amsterdam as part of coordinated protests against the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. "These data centres are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said. Reuters reports: Activist groups have announced actions in 16 countries on Friday and Saturday, according to the "Stop Dirty Data Centers" coalition, which is rallying environmental groups and digital rights campaigns behind calls to pause large-scale construction. In Amsterdam on Friday, more than 100 activists gathered at the construction site of a Microsoft AI data centre, marching arm in arm before breaking into the site, climbing cranes, hanging balloons and dancing while police stood by. Some carried placards with messages reading: "Screw your datacenter."
 
Site owner Pure Data Centers, which plans to invest more than $1 billion and is backed by Brookfield-owned Oaktree, said it was committed to engagement with local stakeholders. "We respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have," it said. Other planned actions include a march in Dublin, a protest outside the parliament building in Warsaw, and a demonstration against a different Microsoft data centre in Denmark. [...] Stop Dirty Data Centers says it is not anti-progress or calling for existing data centers to be closed but that major construction should be halted until governments establish clearer rules.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon Is Locked: Here's What It Means for Your Budget and Your Patch Window
items.author: Ifeoluwa Tech (PhD)
items.content:
If you build software for a living, you probably cannot use it yet. Carbon is going first to a small group of cyber defenders through Google's Fairwind Program while it goes through US government pre-release testing. Developers and businesses get it later, and Google has not said when.

I went through the independent test data, the security research behind Carbon's benchmarks, and Google's own launch notes. Two things matter far more for most of us than who sits at number one. The first is what this class of model will cost to run. The second is what it means for how quickly we need to patch our own code.

What Carbon Costs Per Task

Leaderboards tell you which model scored highest. They rarely tell you what it costs to get that score, and for a startup running agents all day, that is the number that decides whether a model is usable.

Artificial Analysis publishes exactly that. Running its full Intelligence Index, Carbon cost. Claude Opus 5.5 at its highest setting cost $10.04, and GPT-6 Astra at its highest setting cost $6.25.

Scale that to a team running 10,000 hard agent tasks a month and the gap becomes real money:

Model (highest reasoning setting)

A word of caution before anyone builds a budget on this. These are costs on a demanding evaluation suite at standard prices, so your own workload will differ. Treat them as a comparison between models, not a quote. Google is also offering Carbon at half price at launch, $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, before it rises to $4 and $20.

The more interesting detail is why Carbon is cheaper than Opus. It used about 123,000 output tokens per task against 173,000 for Opus 5.5. A model that reaches the answer with fewer tokens saves money on every single call, and for agent loops that run for hours, that adds up faster than any headline discount.

Where It Wins and Where It Doesn't

Carbon is not the best at everything, and the independent data shows where.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, it scored 59, second behind Claude Code running Opus 5.5 at 62. It also came second on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 64%, and on FrontierCode with 51% against 56% for Opus. If your product is mainly an autonomous coding agent, Carbon is a strong option, not an automatic upgrade.

Reliability is the other number to watch. Carbon is more accurate than Google's previous model on the Artificial Analysis knowledge benchmark, but its hallucination rate rose from 4% to 11%. That is still the second lowest of any model tested, behind only Argon. In practice, it means Carbon knows more but guesses more when it does not know. If your app depends on factual answers, keep a verification step in place.

Why It's Gated: Attackers Are Getting Faster

The reason most of us are waiting is in Carbon's cybersecurity scores. Google says it found real vulnerabilities in 88.2% of SEC-bench Pro cases, patched them at the root cause in 71.0% of CWE-bench cases, and turned flaws into working exploits in 54.8% of ExploitGym cases. Those tests were run "without guardrails."

That last benchmark is the uncomfortable one. A model that can turn a bug into an attack is useful to defenders testing their own systems, and just as useful to the people they are defending against.

This did not appear overnight. In 2024, Daniel Kang's group at the University of Illinois showed that GPT-4 could exploit 87% of a set of 15 known vulnerabilities when given the public description, and just 7% without it. Every other model they tested scored zero.

By May 2026, a 16-author team including Dawn Song and Nicholas Carlini had built ExploitGym from 898 real vulnerabilities across userspace programs, Google's V8 engine and the Linux kernel. They found that exploitation is still hard, but frontier agents now succeed on a meaningful share of cases, even with common defences turned on.

Meanwhile, human attackers were already speeding up. Google's Mandiant team exploited in 2023 and found the average time from disclosure to exploitation had fallen to about five days. In 2018 and 2019, it was 63. Seventy per cent were exploited as zero-days, before a patch existed.

Put those two trends together, and the logic behind gating Carbon is easy to follow. Google wants the patching capability in defenders' hands before anything similar becomes widely available. Anthropic made the same call in April when it limited Claude Mythos Preview to its Project Glasswing partners, and has since widened access to about 150 more organisations in more than 15 countries. Neither model is public.

What You Can Do Before It Opens

Here is the part I think matters most. Most teams reading this will not be on a Fairwind or Glasswing list, and attackers will not wait for the general release. So what can a small engineering team actually do this month?

Use what is already available. Gemini 4 Argon has been on the paid Gemini API since 13 October. Google's agent, which upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects as large as 4.5 million lines in its first six months, can be run with public models by any Google Cloud customer, according to Google's.

Patch what is known to be exploited first. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue held as of August 2026. If a dependency you ship is on it, that comes before any new feature.

Prioritise by difficulty, not headlines. Mandiant found no reliable link between media coverage and how fast a bug is exploited. What mattered was how easy the exploit was and how valuable the target. An easy bug in a payment flow deserves more urgency than a famous one that is hard to use.

Assume the window is days, not weeks. Automated dependency updates, fuzzing in your build pipeline and network segmentation all buy time when a patch is not ready.

Ask to get in. Fairwind says it is staged for governments, critical infrastructure and core technology platforms, with more than 650 partners so far. If your company runs infrastructure other people depend on, it is worth asking.

Gating Carbon is the right decision. A strong exploit writer released to everyone on day one would hand attackers a head start that defenders could not close.

But it leaves an open question for the rest of us. Fairwind's published priorities name large institutions. Glasswing's expanded list reached Europe, North America and parts of Asia. Smaller companies, independent researchers and teams in places like Lagos or Nairobi are not clearly covered by either. If the best defensive tools reach well-funded organisations first, the gap between the well-defended and everyone else could widen just as attacks get cheaper.

Until that changes, the practical lesson is simple. Do not wait for the model on top of the leaderboard. Use the tools you can access, patch what attackers are already using, and plan your budget around cost per task rather than rank.

items.title: Developer Pulls Roku's Popular Fish Tank Screensaver Following Fox Sale
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Roku is removing its popular Aquatic Life fish tank screensaver on December 1 and automatically switching affected users to Roku City. According to Cord Cutters News, the creator pulled the license after Roku's sale to FOX was announced. Ars Technica reports: The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn't be renewing Roku's license. "I can't be part of the Fox world," he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News' controversial style of news and entertainment.
 
Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements, according to the user notice. The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS. [...] The decision to not renew the licensing contract has "major financial consequences," Sachs said. "Our needs are very small, with a high property tax bill being the only significant expense," he said. "We'll be okay but can't start any of the projects I had planned."
 
According to Sachs, the licensing "agreement was $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices, or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive. They have always opted for exclusive." Ars asked Roku to confirm the details of the licensing agreement but didn't hear back ahead of publication. The licensing deal with Roku was Sachs' primary form of income, he told Ars, noting low sales of the version of the screensaver for computers. Marine Aquarium fans can still buy the screensaver for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android, but it seems unlikely that it will return to the Roku platform.

items.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.

The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and publicsources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.

We regret to inform you...

Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such information "non-sensitive."

items.title: OpenAI's New Cyber Model Found Ways to Attack Nearly 1,000 Linux Flaws
items.author: BeauHD
items.content: OpenAI says its new GPT-6 Cyber model helped an automated system identify 1,724 security flaws in the Linux kernel and exploit 948 of them to gain administrator-level access during testing, including at least 10 previously unknown techniques. Axios reports: During testing, the system identified 1,724 security flaws and found ways to use 948 of them to gain administrator-level access to Linux systems for about $1.2 million in API credits. At least 10 of the techniques the model used were previously unknown, according to OpenAI. Human researchers reviewed the Linux findings before reporting vulnerabilities and proposed fixes to maintainers. The model also uncovered 81 previously unknown, high-severity flaws in Mozilla's Firefox browser.

items.title: Self-Retrospection Distillation Lifts AI Agent Success From 0% to 60.6% When Every Rollout Fails
items.author: Salesforce $CRM
items.content:
Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight

Haoxiang Zhang, Qinglin Chen, Hiroaki Hayashi, Zhuofeng Li, Siming Zhang, Jiaxin Zhang, Jixuan Chen, Fang Wu, Pan Lu, Silvio Savarese, Julian McAuley, Chien-Sheng Wu (Salesforce AI Research)

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce , which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to 24.2 pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when 37–98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In 2B setting, where 98% of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at 0.0% success, while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction. Code

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a scalable post-training paradigm for large language model (LLM) agents: by executing against automated verifiers and optimizing policies from outcome signals, it enables agents to develop complex, multi-step behavior without human-annotated traces (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). Applied to tool-integrated reasoning (Jin et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2025), code execution (Le et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2026), computer use (Wang et al., 2025a), and multi-agent coordination (Li et al., 2026; Ke et al., 2026), RLVR has proven remarkably effective in settings where agents must act in an external environment and learn from feedback revealed only through interaction.

The supervision in RLVR, however, is inherently retrospective: outcome signals become available only after interaction and are then assigned back to the actions that produced them. Yet a broad line of work on predictive control, world models, and planning suggests that effective interaction also depends on what an agent can anticipate before acting, how its interaction may fail, and what the environment is likely to demand (Pathak et al., 2017; Hafner et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2023). Such pre-interaction expectations shape subsequent exploration, but in RLVR they remain an implicit byproduct of optimizing behavior. More importantly, relying exclusively on post-hoc outcome contrast creates a fundamental blind spot: when all rollouts in a group receive the same reward, especially in long-horizon reasoning tasks where most attempts fail (Lightman et al., 2024), their group-relative advantages vanish (Schulman et al., 2017). The agent may have already revealed rich interactive information about the task and environment, yet learn no signal from that experience.

A recent line of on-policy self-distillation extracts a denser signal from this experience: a single model serves as both teacher and student, with the teacher conditioned on a privileged correct solution and the student trained to match its token-level distribution over the student’s own rollouts (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). Follow-ups vary what the privileged context contains — runtime feedback, skill summaries, or self-revisions — and hybrid objectives fold this signal back into RLVR (Wang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). Across these variants, however, the supervision target is unchanged: hindsight conditions the teacher to sharpen what the agent should do next. We ask instead what the agent could have known — whether the same completed experience can teach it to anticipate, before acting, the demands and failures that only interaction reveals.

We call this : hindsight supervises the agent’s foresight. Given a task, the agent predicts from pre-interaction information alone the knowledge the task may require and the failures it may invite, and the completed trajectory then provides privileged supervision for those predictions.

Building on this principle, we propose Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). For each on-policy trajectory, SRD pairs a pre-interaction prediction with a hindsight prediction conditioned on the completed interaction, and aligns their token-level distributions on the student’s own prospective rollout. As a result, every trajectory can contribute prospective supervision, precisely where reward contrast leaves none: on a failed rollout, the self-teacher’s hindsight lets the agent distill the mistake it just made into an anticipation it can carry forward, and on a saturated all-correct group, the same pairing keeps extracting the knowledge that made those rollouts succeed. Reward thus decides which lesson a trajectory teaches rather than whether it teaches one; learning then continues at both ends of the difficulty range that group-relative methods discard. We make three contributions:

  • A pre-interaction supervision target for agent experience. We formulate prospective learning (§3.1), a post-training target that distills structured information revealed after interaction into predictions constrained to the task and environment context available beforehand, complementary to the retrospective use of experience in RLVR and self-distillation.
  • A composable self-distillation instantiation. Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD, §3.2) adds a lightweight auxiliary objective to RLVR and self-distillation algorithms, and improves performance across diverse tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic settings (§4.2); our analysis characterizes the regimes in which this additional signal is most useful (§5).
  • Learning beyond scalar reward variance. SRD provides dense supervision from all trajectories and remains informative for reward-uniform baselines where RL yields zero advantage (§5).

We consider an agent policy πθ interacting with an environment . Given a task , the agent produces a trajectory τ=(a1,o1,…,aT,oT), where at∼πθ(⋅∣ht) is the action at step t, o_{t}\sim\mathcal{E}(\cdot\mid h_{t},a_{t}) the resulting observation, and ht the previous interaction history.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)

evaluates a completed trajectory with a verifier (e.g. a math checker, unit test, or task rubric), producing a scalar reward r(\tau)=\mathcal{V}(x,\tau) that is converted into an advantage estimate A⁡(τ) and assigned back to the actions that produced it:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RLVR}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Bigl[A(\tau)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\Bigr].

For group-relative methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), given G rollouts {τi}i=1G for the same task with rewards {ri}i=1G, the advantage is A⁡(τi)=(ri−μr)/σr, where μr and σr are the group mean and standard deviation. Critically, when all rollouts receive identical rewards, A⁡(τi)=0 for every i; standard practice discards such uniform-reward groups entirely and resamples until a discriminative batch is obtained (Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), prolonging the rollout and wasting trajectories and whatever information they contain.

Figure 1: Comparison of three paradigms for converting agent experience into training signals. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) scalarizes completed trajectories into outcome rewards and assigns them back to the action policy. Retrospective Learning retains structured post-hoc hindsight to supervise behavior. Prospective Learning uses hindsight to supervise predictions formed from information available before interaction.

Retrospective Learning from Agent Experience.

Beyond scalarizing a trajectory into an outcome, retrospective methods retain structured hindsight z^{\mathrm{hind}}=\mathcal{R}(x,\tau) extracted by a retrospection after interaction—encoding environment feedback, a selected solution, or a reusable skill. All such methods can be unified under a single objective: find a policy πθ that maximizes expected utility when the agent has access to hindsight derived from its own experience,

\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}_{z^{\mathrm{hind}}\sim\mathcal{R}(x,\tau)}\bigl[\mathcal{U}(\pi_{\theta},\,z^{\mathrm{hind}},\,x)\bigr]\Bigr],

where is a method-specific utility that measures how well the policy exploits the hindsight. RLVR is a degenerate instance in which zhind=r⁡(τ) is a scalar and reduces to the advantage-weighted log-likelihood. On-policy self-distillation (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026) sets zhind to a verified trace and to the negative Kullback-Leibler divergence between the hindsight-conditioned teacher and the student:

\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\pi_{\theta},z^{\mathrm{hind}},x)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\Bigl(\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid h_{t},\,z^{\mathrm{hind}})\;\Big\|\;\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\Bigr),

where denotes the stop-gradient self-teacher, instantiated as the same model conditioned on privileged hindsight, and πθ the student conditioned only on the interaction history ht. Skill- and memory-based methods (Wang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026) extract reusable abstractions or reflections as zhind and optimize as downstream task performance.

Despite their differences, these retrospective methods share a common supervision target: post-hoc information is ultimately used to improve the agent’s reasoning or action policy. We next shift the supervision target from the agent takes to what the agent could have anticipated before interaction.

3 Learning Prospectively via Self-Retrospection Distillation

Retrospective learning (Objective 2) uses post-hoc experience zhind to supervise the agent’s reasoning or action policy. We formalize its complementary counterpart: let denote a structured prospection of what the upcoming interaction may unfold. Given a task x and its environment context e, we define the as

p_{\mathrm{fore}}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,e),

without access to the realized interaction. We suppress the specific prospection instruction from the notation; different instantiations may query different aspects of the upcoming interaction.

After interaction, the realized trajectory provides structured hindsight zhind, as defined in Section 2. Prospective learning utilizes this hindsight as privileged context to define a more informed distribution over the same output space:

p_{\mathrm{hind}}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,e,z^{\mathrm{hind}}),

where denotes a hindsight-conditioned teacher policy. Thus, pfore and phind differ in whether post-hoc interaction information is available. Prospective learning optimizes the foresight distribution to anticipate what hindsight reveals:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pro}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\;\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Bigl[D\bigl(p_{\mathrm{hind}}\;\|\;p_{\mathrm{fore}}\bigr)\Bigr].

Unlike retrospective objectives, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pro}} does not optimize the action distribution πθ(⋅∣ht) directly. It trains the agent to internalize, prior to interaction, the patterns of failure and knowledge that its own traces expose: a target remains informative as long as the agent’s anticipation lags behind what its own execution reveals.

Figure 2: Overview of Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). The student policy rolls out trajectories and generates anticipated pitfalls and knowledge foresights via a differently prompted call to the same model. Post-hoc experience from the completed trajectory conditions the stopped-gradient self-teacher, whose token-level distributions supervise the student’s own foresight rollout.

3.2 Self-Retrospection Distillation

We instantiate prospective learning as Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD) with two potential perspectives of foresight: Knowledge, describing knowledge that may be required during interaction, and Pitfall, describing failures that may be encountered. Both views follow the same distillation procedure and differ only in the prospection instruction used to query the model. Within an on-policy rollout group, successful trajectories provide Knowledge supervision, while failed trajectories provide Pitfall supervision, unifying positive and negative interaction experience as two sources of prospective supervision under the same objective. (Footnote: Detailed hindsight, foresight, pitfall, and knowledge prompts are provided in Appendix B.1.)

Hindsight and foresight construction.

For a task x, let {τi}i=1G denote its on-policy rollout group, with verified rewards {ri}. For each rollout i, we use ci to denote its prospective view—Knowledge when ri=1 and Pitfall when ri=0. Let fi=(τi,y∗,ϵi) denote its privileged post-hoc context, where y∗ refers to gold solution or ground-truth answer and ϵi is the corresponding error annotation when applicable. Conditioning on the same view ci, SRD defines a foresight distribution without access to the completed interaction and a hindsight-conditioned distribution that additionally observes fi:

p_{\mathrm{fore}}^{i}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,e,c^{i}),\qquad p_{\mathrm{hind}}^{i}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,e,f^{i},c^{i}).

Here, ci is shorthand for the corresponding prospection instruction. Thus, reward determines the of prospective supervision provided by a rollout, while foresight and hindsight within that view differ only in whether privileged post-hoc interaction information is available.

Hindsight-foresight alignment.

For each rollout, the student samples a foresight sequence zfore,i∼pforei. The hindsight teacher evaluates the same student-generated prefix with access to the post-hoc context fi. SRD minimizes token-level distillation loss over the rollout group:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\{\tau^{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{l=1}^{L_{i}}D\!\left(\pi_{\bar{\theta}}\!\left(\cdot\mid x,e,f^{i},z^{\mathrm{fore},i}_{<l}\right)\;\Big\|\;\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\cdot\mid x,e,z^{\mathrm{fore},i}_{<l}\right)\right)\right],

where D is any distribution divergence measure. A natural and stable choice is the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence, defined for β∈[0,1] as

\mathrm{JSD}_{\beta}(p_{T}\|p_{S})=\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{T}\|m)+(1-\beta)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{S}\|m),\qquad m=\beta\,p_{T}+(1-\beta)\,p_{S},

where p_{T}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,e,f,\,z^{\mathrm{fore}}_{<l}) is the -teacher, instantiated as a stopped-gradient copy of the current policy, and pS=πθ(⋅∣x,e,z<lfore) the student.

We evaluate SRD across four categories and ten tool-integrated reasoning and agentic benchmarks. includes AIME 2024, AIME 2026, and AMO-Bench (Art of Problem Solving, 2026; An et al., 2025); includes LiveCodeBench-v6 (LCB) and OJBench (Jain et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b); includes HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and BrowseComp-Plus (Yang et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2026a); and includes ALFWorld and WebShop (Shridhar et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2022). The evaluation includes held-out distribution, format, and interaction-horizon shifts across domains, testing whether gains transfer beyond the interaction conditions seen during training.

Training & Data Construction.

All methods and model scales are trained on identical data with the same prompt ordering. For , we use DAPO-Math-17K (Yu et al., 2025); for , we train on the split of LCB and evaluate on held-out LCB-v6’s functional-python problems; and for , we follow the Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025a) training recipe and retrieval setup (Jin et al., 2025b) with a fixed toolset follows Zhang et al. (2026a). For tasks, we use the standard training split of ALFWorld and the standard WebShop training partition, evaluating ALFWorld on its OOD split. Math, Code, and Search are jointly trained in a single shuffled mixture, while ALFWorld and WebShop form a second joint training mixture. We train Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B (Team, 2026); full dataset splits, rollout budgets, scaffolds, and optimization hyperparameters are provided in Appendix §C.

We compare against three representative post-training objectives, together with the pretrained policy. uses a DAPO-style (Yu et al., 2025) group-relative policy optimization objective (GRPO; (Shao et al., 2024)) over verified outcome rewards. : on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a baseline following Zhao et al. (2026); Hübotter et al. (2026), where a privileged self-teacher provides token-level supervision to the acting policy; RLSD (Yang et al., 2026) reweighs GRPO with OPSD’s teacher-student divergence. For each baseline we additionally report results, where the privileged prefix is replaced by our structured hindsight zhind and an auxiliary \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} loss is added with weight λ=0.01. Both families are trained with under the filter each objective requires, which we detail in Appendix §C.4.

Table 1: Main results on Math, Code, Search, and Agentic benchmarks, reported as avg​@​8 pass rates in percent. and underline mark the best and second-best result per column within each model scale. Improved Perf. rows give the absolute gain in points that contributes over its own base algorithm, with a deeper green marking a larger gain.

Table 1 reports performance across all task categories, where every row distills the hindsight alone; §5 disentangles the contribution of two perspectives and motivates that choice.

SRD broadly improves post-training objectives and transfers beyond training conditions.

SRD improves category-level performance across GRPO, OPSD, and RLSD at both model scales, with only one regression—WebShop under 9B OPSD (−3.61 pp). The gains are often substantial. For 4B GRPO, adding SRD improves the Math, Code, and Search averages by 10.03, 8.33, and 8.05 pp, respectively, while also improving ALFWorld by 3.25 pp and WebShop by 5.92 pp. The effect extends to other optimization targets: at 9B, OPSD+SRD raises the Math average from 39.70% to 56.92% (+17.22 pp) and Search +10.31 pp. The gains extend to the hybrid objective: RLSD+SRD improves ALFWorld from 66.25% to 77.25% (+11.00 pp). These results indicate that SRD is not tied to a particular base objective, but complements pure RLVR, self-distillation, and their hybrid. The gains also persist when evaluation departs from the training interaction regime. On Code, where training uses the LCB format and evaluation uses functional-format problems, SRD improves the 4B GRPO average by 8.33 pp, including an 8.12 pp gain on OJBench. On the ALFWorld unseen environments, SRD improves every base-objective–scale combination, with gains ranging from 1.12 to 13.74 pp. BrowseComp-Plus further introduces a substantially longer interaction horizon (10× or more tool calls) than the training rollouts; SRD improves five of six settings there, by up to 9.52 pp.

SRD mitigates the instability of pure self-distillation.

Self-distillation without an outcome-grounded signal is the least stable baseline here, and its degradation is concentrated on several tool-integrated benchmarks. At 9B, OPSD alone ends up below the untrained policy — by 5.50 pp on HotpotQA, 3.76 pp on 2Wiki and 2.18 pp on LCB-v6 — i.e. the post-training run has spent its budget degrading the very interface it was supposed to sharpen. The symptom is visible in the scaling behaviour: the Math average of OPSD is across scale, the 9B run landing 2.11 pp the 4B one (39.70% vs. 41.81%), driven by AIME24 (54.17% vs. 62.50%) and AIME26 (52.92% vs. 54.17%). Adding SRD restores the expected ordering and improves both ends: OPSD+SRD reaches 48.11% at 4B and 56.92% at 9B, an 8.81 pp gap in the right direction, gaining 6.30 and 17.22 pp over the corresponding baseline, and all three Math benchmarks now scale monotonically (AIME24 +9.59, AIME26 +10.83, AMO +6.00 pp from 4B to 9B). The same repair shows on the three columns that had regressed below , which now stand at 10.75, 11.75 and 8.54 pp the untrained policy on HotpotQA, 2Wiki and LCB-v6, respectively. These results suggest that prospective supervision provides a complementary learning signal when direct hindsight-to-behavior distillation becomes unstable.

SRD remains effective as the base policy gets stronger.

The benefit of prospective supervision does not disappear at 9B: the best +SRD result increases from 4B to 9B in every task category, with particularly strong improvements in Math and Agentic tasks. Importantly, we observe that the gain from SRD does not increase monotonically with scale, but continues to provide complementary supervision even as the underlying policy becomes stronger. We examine why this signal persists across capability levels in dual-channel SRD in §5, where reward-uniform rollout groups remain prevalent despite a shift from predominantly all-failure to increasingly all-success groups.

Table 2: : Prefix and channel choice in self-distillation, OPSD. Prefix is what the OPSD teacher sees; SRD target is the distilled perspective; green/red marks a gain/loss over the raw-trace no-SRD row, and Wall-clock is the rollout time per step. : the SRD divergence in each perspective during training, on two different domain-shuffled runs on 4B with RLSD; the band is the local interquartile range of the logged points. : which epistemic tokens and the classes they belong to the SRD policy changes. : the GRPO+SRD displacement from the untrained base, decomposed onto GRPO’s own direction: blue is how much of that direction is kept and red is the orthogonal remainder, per split. The dashed line is unity. : per-token similarity between each objective’s own update direction and the same objective plus SRD, as a cumulative distribution over held-out positions, each median marked where its curve crosses 0.5. The arrows give how far each policy travelled from the base before and after adding SRD.

SRD can learn from two different perspectives, and , as we shown the promising results in Table 1 with only the pitfalls channel. In this section, we show this choice is more an efficiency motivation than a performance deficit. In Table 2 (Left), we vary the two things that define that target: what the privileged teacher has in self-distillation (OPSD), and which channel \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} distills alongside it. Read against the no-SRD row of each block, SRD helps under prefixes: distilling pitfalls adds 3.3 and 1.7 pp of AIME26 on the raw-trace prefix at 4B and 9B and 3.3 and 6.7 on the hindsight prefix, and lifts AMO-Bench on 4B with the hindsight prefix by 3.5 pp. The gain concentrates on the hindsight prefix, which solidifies that our hindsight-foresight structure is reliable. However, adding the knowledge channel on top of pitfalls then buys nothing and potentially risks. It is the only setting that ever lands the baseline: 4 pp drops on AMO-Bench at 4B against the baseline, and 62.92% AIME26 at 9B against 65.42%. Its two wins over pitfall are incremental (67.50 vs. 67.08; 26.50 vs. 26.25), and it is the more expensive of the two in every pair, spending more time in rollout, the phase that is 78–87% of one training step. The training curves in Table 2 (top center) make the same point from the optimization side: the pitfall channel’s divergence falls steadily by 47% and 30% over training on the two runs shown, while the knowledge channel stays flat (∼0.0045 and ∼0.003), so the second perspective is somehow redundant and resists being fitted. Therefore, distilling pitfalls alone is a cheaper and safer target.

RQ2: Which Tokens does SRD Reallocate?

In this section, we measure the effect of the SRD on the policy in the context of token categories. We compare GRPO and OPSD against +SRD in the main results (§4.2), respectively, on 5K policies’ own multi-turn rollouts, scoring only the tokens the model itself emitted.

Figure 3: The same shift token by token, on one rollout per arm: rows are the top-4 likeliest continuations under the policy that owns the rollout.

For every token, we accumulate its expected number of occurrences per rollout under the policy that generated the rollout, and take the difference between the two arms (Figure 2, top right); no checkpoint is ever asked to score another’s text. The shift is systematic in the sense that whole lexical classes move together, and in opposite directions. On validation sets in code, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} raises connective prose by 8.6 expected tokens per rollout, explicit planning language (, , ) by 3.7 and words that name the problem’s structure (, , ) by 1.4, while lowering inline mathematical notation by 6.7, punctuation by 4.3, digits by 4.1 and inline variable names (, , ) by 3.0; tool-call syntax remains unchanged (+0.03). The gains and the losses nearly cancel: summed over every class, the shift is +0.6 tokens per rollout, so SRD is not making the policy talk more; it is moving where the policy spends a fixed budget: out of carrying a calculation inline, into naming the problem and the plan, and it leaves the syntax of calling the interpreter untouched. The same redistribution is visible at a single prefix (Figure 3), where it is concentrated: in these two rollouts under GRPO (top) & GRPO+SRD (bottom) the leading continuation moves two to three times as far as the other four (+1.9 against +0.6 nats above, +1.5 against +0.7 below), so \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} re-weights within the local distribution without adding an offset to all of it. Appendix §E.2 has the full class table and two controls: the shift is not a global sharpening, and it does not depend on whose text is scored.

Figure 4: Uniform-reward groups waste most of the rollout at both ends of the capability range: (a) usable share of the budget, (b) overall training group composition.

In GRPO, a prompt contributes a non-zero policy-gradient signal only when its rollout group {τi}i=1G contains reward variation. To isolate this regime, we train on the code domain alone, disable dynamic sampling, and compare the same objective as Yu et al. (2025) with and without SRD across four Qwen3.5 scales (Figure Right). Reward-uniform groups consume a substantial fraction of the sampled budget across capability levels: the usable share of the budget never exceeds 63%, and the discarded share is in capability (98.0, 39.1, 37.0, 41.3 points), because as the policy strengthens all-zero reward groups fall monotonically (98.0→13.4) while all-one reward groups rise monotonically (0.0→27.9): a weak policy solves nothing, a strong one solves a lot, and neither leaves any outcome contrast to learn from. Appendix A.3 formalizes this pattern and shows how heterogeneity in prompt difficulty raises the uniform-group rate beyond the homogeneous prediction. Model scaling does not eliminate the blind spot, but it shifts it from failure saturation toward success saturation. Since \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} scores a trajectory against its own hindsight-conditioned prospection rather than against its peers, it needs no within-group reward variance and applies to every group. The 2B case is the limiting one: with 98% of groups uniform, the baseline’s reward is so sparse that it never gets off the ground (1.6% peak training success, 0.0% final), whereas the same budget with SRD reaches 60.6% in training.

RQ4: How does SRD Shape the Prospection Distribution?

To ask where that change points, we measure all four displacements from one common origin, the untrained base: A and S for what GRPO and OPSD training did (A=log⁡pGRPO−log⁡pbase, and likewise S), and E, ES for the same two runs with SRD. None is a component of another, so we can split E into the part along A and the part across it, E=\alpha\hat{A}+E_{\perp} with , in the Fisher metric (Table 2, bottom center). On the held-out code split (626,992 positions, never trained on), α/∥A∥=1.30: the +SRD run travels 30% along GRPO’s own direction, not back along it, and adds an orthogonal component of comparable size (∥E⟂∥/∥E∥=0.49). Neither this nor its OPSD counterpart averages over cancelling halves: cos⁡(A,E)=+0.81 and cos⁡(S,ES)=+0.98, positive at 77% and 94% of positions individually (Figure 2, bottom right). \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} preserves substantial alignment with the host objective while introducing a non-negligible orthogonal displacement, though the two hosts disagree with each other (cos⁡(A,S)=−0.78). What it changes is scale, in opposite directions: it more than doubles the small RL displacement (0.39→0.86) and shortens the large OPSD one (1.97→0.57) along the same ray (ES≈0.28​S). That asymmetry follows from what the term is — a dense per-token divergence to a target the policy derives from itself. Against a host that supplies sparse credits, it adds movement; against a host already dense self-distillation, it’s a self-referential target competing for the same capacity, and it behaves like an anchor, the run travelling less far along the direction it was already going. With Table 1, where SRD helps under both objectives, the complementarity is measured: an axis extended, an orthogonal component of comparable size, and a step size pulled toward the host’s own. Appendix §E.4 and §E.5 take up the opposite rescaling and the spread across domains.

This section asks what the prospective objective is worth once training is over: whether the choice of distilled channel changes the agentic result, and whether anything further is gained by making the foresight explicit at inference instead of leaving it implicit. Table 3 varies both, under the evaluation protocol of §C.5. In aggregate the answer is narrow. GRPO is the only base objective where the direction is consistent: all four of its SRD arms land above its base, by 1.88–7.63 pp on ALFWorld and 5.92–11.21 pp on WebShop. Under RLSD the sign flips with the channel: Pitfall is worth +5.75 pp while adding Knowledge costs 6.88 pp against the same base, plausibly because RLSD already carries a self-distillation term and the Knowledge channel adds a second self-referential target competing with it, though with two objectives at one scale and one seed we can only offer that as a conjecture. The test-time axis is nearly inert: of the four checkpoints, one gains 5.00 pp when it states its foresight before acting and the other three move by 2, 3 and 11 rollouts out of 800, which we read as no change, not as a measured cost. What the aggregate hides matters more than what it shows. Not one of the eight arms improves all six ALFWorld task types over its own base; every arm trades, without exception. The spread between an arm’s best and worst task type runs from 10.16 pp, for the flattest arm (GRPO+SRD (Pitfall)), to 60.07 pp, and the same task type moves in opposite directions depending on the arm: across the eight, ranges from −20.13 to +40.28 pp and from −27.08 to +9.38 pp. Avg therefore hides the trade. Neither axis buys a uniform improvement, and the test-time one carries an extra risk: a predicted foresight can be wrong, and the one we examine is, placing a two-object task’s capacity limit on the destination instead of the agent (§F.3). As a training target a wrong foresight can be corrected by subsequent updates; spoken before acting, it conditions the whole episode. Generating it at inference is therefore not free.

RLVR learns from verifiable trajectory-level outcomes (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), while process supervision raises the temporal resolution of that feedback (Lightman et al., 2024; Setlur et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025). A parallel line increases the information content retained from each completed rollout: on-policy self-distillation conditions a self-teacher on privileged solutions (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026), and its successors enrich that privileged context with self-revisions (He et al., 2026), trajectory-level skills (Wang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026), procedural memory (Liu et al., 2026), or an outcome-RL term (Yang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Recent diagnostics, however, show that enriching the teacher context is not unconditionally beneficial: privileged conditioning can alter calibration, self-correction, epistemic suppression, and even the teacher behavior being distilled (Zhang et al., 2026b; Kaur et al., 2026; Ichihara et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). These motivate separating two design choices that prior work conflates — and what hindsight supervises. Across all of the above, the supervision target is the same (the agent’s action distribution); SRD changes the target, redirecting hindsight from behavior to foresight.

Prospective Learning and Foresight.

Learning to anticipate the consequences of interaction has a long history in reinforcement learning. Early predictive and model-based methods learn from realized transitions to estimate future outcomes and support planning before execution (Sutton, 1988; Sutton, 1990), while later world-model approaches explicitly imagine possible futures — from learned “dreams” and latent dynamics to decision-relevant predictions used for planning (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020; Schrittwieser et al., 2020). Complementary hindsight methods reuse realized outcomes to relabel or assign credit to past experience (Andrychowicz et al., 2017; Chelu et al., 2020). Recent language-agent work has brought these ideas closer together by learning action consequences, prospective state rollouts, and other forms of foresight before execution (Xie et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2026c). SRD follows this predictive lineage but couples hindsight and foresight differently: completed interaction provides privileged training-time supervision for a trajectory-blind prediction of interaction-relevant structure. Thus, SRD does not require reconstructing a full future trajectory or explicitly consuming foresight for planning at inference time; hindsight teaches the shared policy what could have been anticipated before acting.

We introduced prospective learning, extending the use of post-hoc experience from behavioral revision to pre-interaction anticipation. Our proposed Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD) instantiates this principle by distilling hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight over interaction-relevant knowledge and failure modes. Empirically, SRD complements reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and self-distillation across diverse reasoning and agentic tasks, including regimes where objective-specific filtering leaves much of the sampled experience unused. More broadly, we view prospective learning as a post-training design axis, and we believe that a key direction toward more capable agents is to optimize not only how they learn from experience, but also how well they can anticipate what an interaction will demand and where it may fail before acting.

This work studies post-training for language-model agents on mathematical reasoning, programming, retrieval, and simulated interactive tasks. Improved task performance can also increase the effectiveness of agents used for harmful purposes, including unsafe code execution or unauthorized information access. Distilling a model’s own hindsight can reinforce errors and biases from its base model, training data, or feedback; benchmark gains therefore do not establish safety, fairness, or reliability in deployment. Applications beyond the evaluated settings should use task-specific safety evaluations, sandboxed execution, restricted tool permissions, and human oversight for consequential actions, with safeguards for sensitive information in interaction traces.
