items.title: Will Open-Source Software Survive the AI Vulnerability Flood?
items.author: Sebastian Martinez Torregrosa
items.content:
Why the AI-driven vulnerability flood could hit open-source maintainers harder today—and leave surviving projects more secure tomorrow.

We may be entering the largest vulnerability discovery wave in software history. AI is making it practical to examine billions of lines of legacy code more thoroughly and continuously, reassessing their security as they interact with new components and environments. One potential consequence is a sharp increase in reported vulnerabilities, and some projects are already experiencing the pressure.

But open source appears to be facing this wave earlier and more visibly than closed source. Does that mean proprietary software is more secure in the age of AI?

And can open-source projects survive the flood?

The more interesting question is what happens after it.

  1. Software complexity makes vulnerability discovery a universal challenge. Vulnerabilities can emerge from interactions between components, dependencies, and changing environments—even when the underlying code has not changed. Continuous security reassessment, using evolving AI capabilities, is essential across both open- and closed-source software.
  2. The AI-driven vulnerability flood will be a temporary peak, not permanent growth. AI-assisted analysis will progressively deplete the finite backlog of detectable historical vulnerabilities, while continuous security analysis in development and CI/CD will reduce its replenishment. Vulnerability discovery will continue, but at a lower rate once the initial backlog has been substantially examined.
  3. Open-source projects may face the flood before they can adapt. Easier access to source code and broader independent scrutiny could accelerate vulnerability discovery, overwhelming individual maintainers and communities whose security-response capacity cannot scale quickly enough.
  4. Open-source software could become more secure, but its ecosystem will face growing pressure to reorganize. AI-driven vulnerability discovery and growing security obligations could expose the longstanding fragility of critical dependencies maintained by small, underfunded communities. The resulting pressure may accelerate funding changes, consolidation, and project abandonment—potentially producing more secure surviving projects, but a less diverse ecosystem with new concentrations of systemic risk.
  5. Closed source is not necessarily safer—it may simply face the flood later. Restricted access to code and binaries can delay independent discovery and reduce public visibility, potentially leaving historical vulnerabilities undiscovered and unfixed for longer. Internal vendor analysis can alter this trajectory.
  6. More public vulnerabilities today could mean fewer exploitable vulnerabilities tomorrow. Broad AI-assisted scrutiny of open-source code may accelerate the discovery and elimination of historical vulnerabilities. Closed-source software may retain a larger hidden backlog for longer, while attackers can independently discover and exploit vulnerabilities regardless of public disclosure. Higher CVE counts may therefore reflect faster elimination of hidden risks, not inherently less secure software.
  7. Enterprises must accelerate remediation from patch creation to production. AI compresses the discovery-to-exploitation window, making traditional patch deployment timelines increasingly dangerous. Automated testing, cloud-native rolling updates, user-space live patching, and high-availability clustering can reduce deployment delays without sacrificing service continuity.

Every mature codebase carries an unknown number of undiscovered vulnerabilities. Some were introduced recently. Many have existed for years or decades.

Traditional security research was always constrained by human time and expertise, so the number of vulnerabilities reported was never a reliable measure of the number that existed.

A project with ten CVEs was not necessarily less secure than one with none; it may simply have been examined more carefully.

AI changes the economics of that examination. Analysis that once required sustained expert attention can increasingly be automated, repeated, and applied across large codebases.

Historically, discovering or disclosing a vulnerability did not necessarily make it immediately exploitable at scale. Some vulnerabilities may already have been exploited privately as zero-days for years before public discovery or disclosure. Developing a reliable exploit often required specialized expertise and considerable time. AI is eroding that barrier. It can accelerate exploit development, automate parts of the exploitation process, and make sophisticated attacks accessible to a much broader range of attackers. The interval between vulnerability discovery and widespread exploitation could shrink dramatically, potentially approaching zero for some classes of vulnerabilities.

The more intensively software is examined, the worse its reported security can initially appear—not because the code has changed, but because previously invisible defects are becoming visible.

A Temporary Peak, Not a Permanent Elevation

For relatively stable codebases, the result should be a temporary peak in vulnerability discovery rather than a permanently elevated discovery rate.

AI-assisted analysis first encounters the accumulated backlog. Discoveries accelerate. Mature projects that reported relatively few issues may suddenly generate substantial numbers.

As detectable legacy flaws are progressively discovered, the remaining backlog of undiscovered vulnerabilities should eventually shrink. Whether the software actually becomes safer depends on how quickly those discoveries are converted into effective fixes.

The prediction is that the initial discovery flood will be temporary, not that vulnerability discovery will eventually stop. Its timing, magnitude, and duration will differ across projects, languages, and ecosystems.

A similar possibility was raised by, which suggested that AI-driven vulnerability discovery could eventually exhaust much of the readily discoverable historical backlog, while AI-assisted security testing during development could help reduce future vulnerability accumulation.

Software continues to change. New features, dependencies, architectural shifts, and AI-generated code can introduce fresh vulnerabilities. Even unchanged legacy code may become exploitable when combined with new components or exposed in different environments. Vulnerabilities can also emerge from interactions between individually secure components, making security a property of the integrated system, not just its individual parts. This makes continuous reassessment necessary across both open- and closed-source software, not merely repeated analysis of newly written code.

Continuous reassessment must also evolve with AI itself. As AI analysis improves, it may identify vulnerability classes, attack paths, and complex interactions that earlier generations of tools could not detect—even in code that has not changed. A completed security scan therefore represents an assessment using the capabilities available at that time, not a permanent declaration that the software is secure.

The historical backlog accumulated over decades when comprehensive security analysis was expensive and largely dependent on human expertise. New software will increasingly be developed under very different conditions.

As AI-assisted vulnerability detection becomes integrated into CI/CD pipelines, newly written code can be examined continuously, allowing vulnerabilities to be discovered and corrected before they reach production or accumulate into another historical backlog.

For this reduction to be sustainable, AI-assisted vulnerability detection must eventually become a commodity: an affordable, routine part of software development rather than an expensive, separately commissioned security activity. Finding and fixing vulnerabilities while code is still being written is far cheaper than discovering them years after deployment, when remediation may require coordinated disclosure, backports, and production patching.

This security analysis must also remain distinct from AI-assisted code generation. Both can coexist in the same development workflow, but generating code and independently evaluating its security are different responsibilities. Vulnerability detection requires dedicated security-focused tools and AI systems trained or optimized for that purpose. Just as compilation does not replace testing, an AI system that produces code should not be relied upon as its sole security reviewer.

AI therefore creates two opposing pressures on vulnerability accumulation. AI-assisted coding can accelerate the introduction of new vulnerabilities as software production scales, potentially sustaining elevated discovery rates even after much of the historical backlog has been examined. Continuous, independent AI-assisted security analysis during development can counteract that effect by identifying and correcting vulnerabilities before they reach production. Without that second mechanism, the predicted decline in vulnerability discovery rates may never materialize.

Not every defect will be detected. But the most readily detectable vulnerabilities should increasingly be identified and eliminated during development rather than accumulating unnoticed for years.

This creates two complementary mechanisms: AI-driven discovery and remediation reduce the historical vulnerability backlog, while continuous AI-assisted security analysis limits its replenishment.

AI-assisted vulnerability detection should therefore become a continuous, standard part of CI/CD pipelines, rather than an occasional security assessment.

AI detection capabilities will continue improving, but their effectiveness need not grow exponentially forever. As techniques mature and become widely adopted, the most readily detectable vulnerabilities should become progressively less common in both legacy and newly developed code.

The expected outcome is therefore an initial discovery flood followed by a smaller, continuous flow of newly discovered vulnerabilities—not the disappearance of vulnerabilities altogether.

New vulnerability classes, major architectural changes, and uneven adoption could produce further discovery waves. But they do not necessarily imply that the enormous historical backlog can be recreated at the same rate.

A lasting reduction in the total vulnerability stock requires effective elimination to exceed the introduction of new vulnerabilities.

Discovery enables elimination; it does not itself reduce the total stock.

Three quantities must be kept distinct.

is the identification of a vulnerability. is its public reporting. is its effective removal from the software.

CVE counts track a subset of publicly recorded vulnerabilities. They miss vulnerabilities found and fixed internally without public assignment of an identifier.

Residual vulnerability stock is also not the same as residual security risk. Severity, exploitability, exposure, and available mitigations matter. A hundred obscure issues in unreachable code may represent less practical risk than one remotely exploitable flaw in an exposed service.

One curve describes the rate at which vulnerabilities are discovered. Another describes the residual stock of vulnerabilities that remain.

These curves do not necessarily move together.

A surge in discoveries can coexist with a falling residual stock if vulnerabilities are eliminated faster than new ones are introduced. Conversely, a low discovery rate can coexist with a stable or growing vulnerability stock if scrutiny is limited or remediation lags. The discovery curve alone cannot establish whether software is becoming more secure.

Public CVE disclosures provide an imperfect observable indicator of the first curve, not a direct measurement of it.

In open source, the discovery curve is hypothesized to rise earlier and more sharply for three reasons:

  • First, source code makes large-scale AI-assisted analysis easier, although AI can also analyze binaries.
  • Second, open-source code is generally accessible to independent researchers and automated systems, while proprietary binaries, historical versions, and patches may be less readily available.
  • Third, open-source discoveries and remediation are often more publicly visible, while proprietary vendors can handle some findings internally before public disclosure.

This could also produce a more visible peak in public disclosures, although the two trajectories need not be identical.

A further accelerator is independent scrutiny by downstream users. Open-source projects are not analyzed only by their maintainers or security researchers. Commercial manufacturers and integrators also have incentives to examine the components they depend on, reinforced by regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act, which establishes security responsibilities across their software supply chains. AI makes such analysis increasingly affordable and repeatable. Even a small project could therefore face continuous scrutiny from many independent organizations, accelerating the discovery of historical vulnerabilities while helping detect new ones before another backlog accumulates. Projects that can keep pace may become substantially more secure. Those that cannot may struggle to survive.

The same visibility can accelerate independent investigation and remediation through upstream fixes, forks, and downstream patches without waiting for a single vendor.

Neither advantage is guaranteed.

Limited maintainer capacity can turn a discovery surge into a growing backlog of known but unfixed vulnerabilities. Well-resourced proprietary vendors may remediate internal findings faster.

Proprietary software could experience a lower, later, and less visible peak in public vulnerability statistics. But that does not necessarily imply a lower rate of actual discovery. Its source is generally available to fewer external researchers, while well-resourced vendors can conduct extensive internal AI-assisted analysis, discover vulnerabilities, and remediate them before public disclosure.

Furthermore, delaying discovery does not eliminate the underlying vulnerabilities. If the historical backlog is examined and remediated more slowly, vulnerabilities may remain undiscovered and unfixed for longer. A lower public disclosure rate, reflected in fewer CVEs, can therefore coexist with a larger hidden vulnerability backlog, although extensive internal security analysis by proprietary vendors can change that outcome.

A hidden vulnerability backlog is not necessarily a safer one. Public disclosure can increase immediate exploitation risk by enabling parallel attacks, but it also creates an opportunity for remediation. Once a vulnerability is effectively eliminated, that particular exposure ends. By contrast, vulnerabilities that remain undiscovered or unremediated can persist for years, while attackers may independently discover and exploit them without any public disclosure. If broader AI-assisted scrutiny allows open-source projects to discover and eliminate their historical vulnerabilities earlier, they may accept greater short-term exposure in exchange for fewer long-term attack opportunities.

AI can still analyze binaries, compare patched and unpatched versions, and probe running systems. Closed source is not immune. The practical difference is often whether an attacker has access to the binary itself or only remote interaction with a running system.

Once sufficient technical information is available, unpatched deployments face similar exposure to AI-assisted exploitation regardless of the original licensing model. Proprietary vendors can still retain advantages in controlling the distribution of fixes and aspects of disclosure coordination.

Closed source also rarely means pure closed source. Most commercial products depend on substantial amounts of open-source code, and many proprietary vendors participate in upstream projects.

Those vendors cannot fully control the vulnerability discovery and disclosure timelines of their dependencies.

AI-driven vulnerability discovery creates four immediate pressures—and a critical challenge:

  1. Misleading public metrics: A surge in reported vulnerabilities can make software appear less secure even while its residual vulnerability stock is declining.
  2. Compressed response windows: Exploitation can outpace patch development and deployment.
  3. Production deployment bottlenecks: Traditional testing, change management, and downtime requirements delay security updates.
  4. Regulatory and disclosure pressure: Vulnerability-handling obligations and coordinated disclosure add operational complexity.

The critical challenge is having no time to adapt. Open-source communities, individual maintainers, and enterprise teams must adapt to security-response timelines far shorter than those they are accustomed to, while already facing an accelerating vulnerability flood. Many lack the automation, resources, or capacity to make that transition quickly enough.

AI can shorten the time from discovery to exploitation. It can also shorten the time required to develop a fix.

The production deployment lag, however, largely predates AI.

Enterprise testing, validation, and change-management processes still take time. The danger is that attackers may increasingly exploit vulnerabilities faster than organizations can deploy remediation.

Even when fixes are available, delays in processing security advisories and identifying affected downstream dependencies can postpone remediation before production deployment even begins ().

As AI compresses the interval between discovery and exploitation, potentially to near zero, traditional response timelines become increasingly untenable. Maintainers may need to investigate, develop, validate, and release fixes within hours rather than days or weeks. Enterprises face the same pressure to test and deploy those fixes into production with minimal delay. For the most critical, readily exploitable vulnerabilities, security response may need to approach real-time operations rather than periodic patch management.

The response must be to aggressively compress the traditional patch workflow from development to production. Automated QA, regression testing, and deployment validation can shorten the time needed to release fixes safely. Once fixes are available, technologies that minimize service disruption can accelerate their deployment into production: cloud-native workloads designed for rolling restarts without service interruption, user-space live patching beyond the Linux kernel, and high-availability clustering for traditional applications. The objective is not merely to produce patches faster, but to deploy them into production before attackers can exploit the vulnerabilities they address.

Coordinated disclosure remains useful, but it cannot guarantee secrecy. Leaks, independent discoveries, public patch analysis, and active exploitation can all shorten the preparation window.

Open-source communities can respond through parallel investigation, but actual response speed depends on available expertise, coordination, and maintainer capacity.

When this discovery surge coincides with growing regulatory requirements, weaker projects, communities, and smaller companies may face genuine viability risks.

The introduces security and vulnerability-handling obligations for covered products with digital elements, including requirements relating to vulnerability management, security updates, and reporting of certain actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents.

These obligations do not apply uniformly. Non-commercial open-source development is treated differently from commercial products, while qualifying open-source software stewards have a distinct framework.

Commercial vendors incorporating open-source components may nevertheless face obligations that increase expectations placed on upstream projects.

Meanwhile, the cost of triaging genuine vulnerabilities alongside noisy, low-quality, or AI-generated reports can overwhelm limited maintainer capacity.

Even projects that successfully improve their security may struggle with the financial and operational costs of the transition.

Can All Open-Source Projects Survive?

Open-source projects and maintainers will face five growing pressures:

  1. An unprecedented volume of vulnerability findings.
  2. Triage, prioritization, coordinated disclosure, and remediation.
  3. Continuous AI reassessment: Repeatedly scanning existing and new code as detection capabilities evolve.
  4. Helping downstream users deploy security fixes rapidly, including through compatibility with rolling updates, live patching, or high-availability environments where applicable.
  5. Continuously assessing the security and sustainability of critical third-party dependencies, particularly those maintained by small, underfunded communities.

Together, these pressures increase the cost and complexity of maintaining open-source software, potentially beyond what smaller communities can sustain.

The discovery flood will not affect every project equally. A well-funded project with dedicated security engineers, automated testing, and established vulnerability-response processes is in a very different position from a small community maintaining millions of lines of legacy code.

Many widely used open-source dependencies are maintained by small, underfunded communities, sometimes by a single volunteer. This is not a new problem: critical software infrastructure often depends on projects with very limited maintenance resources, creating systemic dependencies whose importance far exceeds the capacity of the communities supporting them. The imbalance between commercial dependence on these components and financial support for their maintenance has been discussed for years.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, combined with downstream compliance pressures from regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), could amplify this existing weakness. External researchers may soon be able to identify dozens of plausible vulnerabilities in days, while each report still requires validation, prioritization, remediation, and testing. Discovery capacity can scale dramatically without a corresponding increase in maintainer resources.

Automation can help. AI-assisted initial triage, duplicate detection, reproducibility checks, and severity assessment can reduce the burden of processing vulnerability reports. Maintainers can prioritize issues according to exploitability, exposure, and practical impact rather than treating every reported finding as equally urgent.

Integrating AI-assisted vulnerability detection into CI/CD pipelines can also prevent newly introduced vulnerabilities from accumulating into another historical backlog. But this addresses the future flow of vulnerabilities, not the immediate cost of investigating and remediating decades of existing defects.

Continuous security reassessment also introduces a recurring cost. As AI detection capabilities evolve, projects will need to re-examine existing code, not just newly introduced changes. Running increasingly sophisticated analysis, validating findings, and maintaining the necessary infrastructure will require resources that smaller communities may struggle to sustain.

The pressure extends beyond discovering and fixing vulnerabilities. Projects may also need to make security updates easier for their users to deploy, reducing the operational friction that leaves known vulnerabilities unpatched in production. Depending on the software, this may require supporting rolling updates, user-space live patching, or integration with high-availability clustering. These capabilities can reduce service disruption, but developing, testing, and maintaining them adds another cost that not every project can absorb.

And automation has limits. A project may receive more genuine findings than its maintainers can investigate, validate, fix, and release—even after substantially improving its processes.

Some projects will adapt. Others may need additional commercial support, foundation funding, shared security infrastructure, or new maintainers. Some may not survive the transition.

The ability to discover vulnerabilities is scaling faster than the capacity of every open-source community to remediate them.

Improving the security of open-source software does not guarantee the survival of the projects maintaining it.

The risk is systemic, not merely local to individual projects. A vulnerability in a widely reused, poorly maintained component can affect thousands of downstream products. The 2024 XZ Utils backdoor demonstrated how weaknesses in the maintenance and trust structure of a small upstream project could threaten major downstream projects, including Linux distributions, even though the incident involved a supply-chain compromise rather than an AI-driven vulnerability-discovery flood.

Even if the upstream project disappears, its software may remain embedded in production systems without security maintenance. AI-assisted discovery could expose these shared weaknesses at scale, turning the limited remediation capacity of a small upstream community into a security bottleneck for entire software supply chains. Greater reliance on fewer surviving projects could further concentrate systemic risk.

AI-driven vulnerability discovery may act as an evolutionary pressure on open source. Projects capable of adapting can emerge stronger and more secure, while those unable to keep pace risk disappearing. The result may be more secure surviving projects, but also a less diverse ecosystem with greater concentration of systemic risk.

The discovery flood could leave four lasting consequences:

  1. Effective remediation reduces historical vulnerabilities, while continuous AI reassessment limits the accumulation of new ones.
  2. Higher security standards: Continuous AI analysis and faster, less disruptive remediation become normal expectations for software maintenance.
  3. A lower vulnerability discovery rate: Once the historical backlog is substantially examined, vulnerability discovery will stabilize at a lower, continuous rate.
  4. A less diverse ecosystem: Rising maintenance costs may favor well-funded projects while threatening smaller communities.

The predicted discovery peak creates an opportunity for surviving projects to eliminate a substantial portion of their detectable legacy vulnerabilities. Whether that opportunity translates into improved security depends on sufficient remediation capacity.

The security benefit extends beyond publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. Undiscovered or privately discovered vulnerabilities may already be exploitable, including by attackers who never disclose them. Eliminating the historical backlog therefore reduces potential attack opportunities, not merely future CVE counts. The value of earlier discovery and remediation is that vulnerabilities can be removed before attackers exploit them—or before additional attackers independently discover them.

And if AI-assisted security analysis becomes a normal part of development pipelines, those projects may be less likely to accumulate comparable backlogs again.

This transition will also raise the baseline expectations for software maintenance. Continuous AI-assisted security reassessment, automated vulnerability triage, and faster remediation will increasingly become standard practices rather than optional investments. Users will also expect security updates that can be deployed with minimal service disruption. Meeting these expectations will require sustained engineering investment, even after the initial vulnerability flood subsides.

The most heavily scrutinized codebases may no longer be those with the largest remaining vulnerability stock. They may be those in which the greatest proportion of detectable historical defects has already been eliminated.

Raw CVE counts would then become an increasingly misleading comparative metric.

Comparing ecosystems by the number of vulnerabilities they report in a given year risks rewarding opacity and penalizing transparency.

But the benefits may not be distributed equally.

The projects that survive may increasingly be those backed by commercial vendors, large foundations, or organizations capable of sustaining continuous security operations.

Open-source software could emerge more secure from the transition, while the ecosystem maintaining it becomes less diverse.

These predictions are testable and falsifiable, but they concern different outcomes.

  • The temporary discovery peak would be challenged if vulnerability discovery rates remain persistently elevated in mature, extensively analyzed codebases, or if continuous AI-assisted analysis fails to prevent newly introduced vulnerabilities from accumulating into another substantial backlog.
  • The open-versus-closed-source trajectory would be challenged if proprietary ecosystems demonstrate equally early and extensive vulnerability discovery through internal AI-assisted analysis, rather than experiencing a delayed discovery wave.
  • The long-term security improvement depends on effective remediation. It would be undermined if discovered vulnerabilities remain unfixed or if elimination fails to outpace the introduction of new vulnerabilities.

A decline in reported CVEs alone would not prove depletion. It could reflect reduced research activity, changes in disclosure practices, or declining analysis coverage.

A dramatic increase in reported vulnerabilities does not necessarily mean software is becoming less secure. It may mean that decades of accumulated defects are finally being found.

Unlike the past, however, future software development could increasingly detect those defects before they become another generation of accumulated security debt.

Whether this discovery wave leaves open source weaker or stronger depends on which projects and companies can convert the findings into fixes before the peak exhausts them.

**The software reporting the most vulnerabilities today may be the software whose hidden vulnerabilities are disappearing fastest—provided it survives long enough for the cleanup to matter.**

items.title: Tesla to Wind Down Cybertruck Production
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Elon Musk says Tesla will be "winding down" Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027 to free up capacity for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi. CNBC reports: The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said.
 
The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000. "Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different." While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Thank you Slashdot reader Dan Posluns for sharing the news.

items.title: AI Is Finding More Software Vulnerabilities Than Humans Can Verify
items.author: Alex Vainer
items.content:
Starting today, if you report a low or medium severity vulnerability to curl, it does not go to the security team. It goes into a public GitHub issue queue with everything else.

Daniel Stenberg announced the change on October 20. His reason is worth reading closely, because it is not the reason you would guess: “This policy change is entirely triggered by the current avalanche of vulnerability reports that keep pouring in.” Over the last few years, he notes, more than 90% of submissions could quickly be assessed as less than high severity.

Two days later he published something that complicates every story written about AI and open source in the last eighteen months, including mine. “Since spring 2026 the slop reports are practically gone,” he wrote. Recent months have brought hundreds of vulnerability reports and “every single one had AI involved to some extent.” His assessment of them: “I personally don’t refer to this as AI slop because the reports are typically accurate and correct, even if much too wordy.”

And then the line that should end the lazy version of this conversation: “Ignoring real vulnerabilities because they were found by AI does not make users safe and secure. It makes them vulnerable.”

So the quality problem got solved. The reports are real. And the maintainer of one of the most widely deployed pieces of software on earth just moved ninety percent of his intake onto the public commons anyway.

That is the story of October, and it is not a story about slop.

The lab hit the same wall first

On October 8, Anthropic launched a free vulnerability scanner for open-source projects. Buried in the announcement is the most candid thing a frontier lab has said this year:

“We have discovered over 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities, but have only been able to manually review and triage approximately 6,000 of these. While 6,000 vulnerabilities is significant, we remain bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings.”

Read that again. The company with the model that found the bugs could not keep up with the bugs its model found.

Their resolution was to stop trying. The scanner’s reports are, in their own words on the Cyber Mission page, “model-generated and sent without human review. That means maintainers receive them faster, but it also means that some will contain inaccuracies.” The quality bar is an expectation rather than a measurement: “We expect a true-positive rate above 90%.”

The scanner FAQ contains a sentence I find genuinely admirable and also damning: they will not impose a disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings because “we do not feel comfortable forcing maintainers to carefully read each finding if we have not yet done the same.”

They know exactly what they are handing over. They said so.

The scoreboard nobody quotes

Anthropic publishes a live disclosure dashboard, which is more transparency than most of this industry offers, so the numbers below are to their credit as data even as they are the problem.

As of October 2: 29,439 candidate vulnerabilities found. Around 6,123 reviewed by external security firms. 6,157 disclosed to maintainers, of which 4,824 went out direct and unvalidated. 5,103 acknowledged.

That is 8.4% of what was disclosed, and under 2% of what was found. The dashboard is careful to note that patch counts lag, which is true and fair. It is still the clearest picture available of where the work stops.

The pattern repeats one level up. Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program announcement on October 6 reported “at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026” from its partners. The announcement contains no total for how many were fixed, and explains why: “fewer than 50% of partners disclosed patched numbers, often because their fixes were still in progress.”

Finding is now a volume business. Fixing is still a cottage industry.

Google just closed the door

On October 1, Google paused new product vulnerability reports to its open-source reward program, pointing to a rise in automated submissions. It is worth being precise here, because the lazy version of this story is everywhere: Google did not say those submissions were AI-generated, and gave no figures. Supply-chain reports still go through, and an update is promised in the first quarter of 2027.

curl pushed the cost onto a public queue. Anthropic pushed it onto maintainers. Google shut the intake. Three different institutions, one month, same decision.

Here is where it stops being a security story.

Fiona Chen and James Stratton of Harvard analyzed roughly 300 million work events across 718 firms and 725,938 workers, using engineering telemetry spanning January 2021 to March 2026, to measure what AI coding agents actually changed. Their paper is a job-market paper rather than a peer-reviewed publication, hosted on the author’s own site, and the data comes from Jellyfish, a vendor that sells engineering analytics to the firms in the sample. Weigh it accordingly. It is still the largest measurement of its kind that exists.

What adoption produced: “30% for lines of code, 20% for commits, and 23% for pull requests.”

What it did not produce: any detectable increase in finished work. For resolved issues the estimate was 0.12 per worker-month against a baseline of 3.67, with a standard error of 0.17, which is statistically indistinguishable from nothing. Completed epics, the same. Their confidence intervals “allow us to rule out effects larger than 12% of the baseline mean.”

Where the time went: the path from pull request to merge lengthened 49%, from about seven days to over ten. The share of pull requests with changes requested rose from 0.13 to 0.25, close to double. Comments per pull request rose 35%. The share of workers doing code review rose 14%.

Output up a third. Delivered work flat. Everybody in the review queue.

A junior engineer quoted in the paper describes the texture of it better than the regressions do: “People could make a huge number of commits quickly, but code review was still the bottleneck. He could only review my code once a week. After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks.”

The statistic that explains everything

Of all the numbers in that paper, one stopped me.

As of March 2026, nearly in the sample had used AI tools somewhere in the code review process. And yet only 23.3% of review comments were AI-generated, and only 10.8% of pull requests received even one AI comment.

The tools were bought. The tools were installed. And when the actual checking had to happen, humans did roughly nine-tenths of it anyway.

That is not a capability gap. These are the same models that wrote the code and found the 29,000 vulnerabilities. It is a trust gap, and it is the whole economics of this moment compressed into two percentages. We deployed AI enthusiastically on the half of the work that produces something visible, and we quietly kept humans on the half that decides whether the visible thing is real.

Two corrections to the story I would otherwise be tempted to tell.

This is not a safety crisis. VulnCheck found that of 1,061 vulnerabilities attributed to AI-assisted discovery, 14 had been exploited in the wild. That is 1.3%, which they note is “roughly matching the overall exploitation rate” for everything else, and they say explicitly that their data does not suggest AI-discovered vulnerabilities are more likely to be exploited. The cost here is labor, not danger. Anyone selling you danger is selling something.

This is not an argument against AI vulnerability research. It works. Models found a real high-severity flaw in curl that Stenberg shipped a fix for in October, and he has called the current generation of findings genuinely better than what traditional analyzers produced. Refusing the findings would be worse than receiving them. He said so, and he is right.

One real asymmetry does show up in the data. VulnCheck’s audit of the disclosure ledger found the model rated 91.5% of its findings critical or high, while maintainers who reviewed them rated 51.3% that way. The machine is not making things up. It is reliably more alarmed than the person who has to act.

The thing to actually watch

In September I argued that AI drove the cost of producing a claim to zero without touching the cost of checking one, and that verification had quietly become an unpaid tax. I thought the open question was who would end up paying it.

October answered: nobody pays it. It gets moved.

The lab moved it to the maintainer. The maintainer moved it to the public queue. Google moved it out of the building. Inside companies, the engineer who used to write code moved it to the senior engineer who now spends 49% longer getting a change merged. At each step the person handing it off is acting reasonably, and the cost is undiminished, and it is always someone else’s week.

So if you run anything that consumes AI output, and at this point that is everyone, the question worth asking is not what your tools can generate. It is who verifies it, whether that person agreed to, and what happens when they stop. I build and run these systems every day, and my own audit is uncomfortable reading: the generation side of my stack is instrumented and fast, and the checking side is me.

The bottleneck did not disappear when we automated production. It just stopped being visible from the side of the pipe that gets celebrated.

items.title: Gate Technology Ltd CEO Dr. Giovanni Cunti Presents Gate Pay at AIBC World Rome 2026
items.author: Blockman PR and Marketing
items.content:
On November 4, at the AIBC World Rome 2026 summit held in Rome, Dr. Giovanni Cunti, CEO of Gate Technology Ltd, was invited to attend a featured panel discussion. Dr. Cunti noted that Gate is authorised by the Malta Financial Services Authority (MFSA) as a Crypto-Asset Service Provider (CASP) under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) and as a Financial Institution (FI), and that Gate is moving from regulatory compliance towards operational execution and real-world use cases.

Reflecting on over a year of operating under the framework, Dr. Cunti emphasized: “MiCA has effectively bridged the gap with legacy finance and created a unified ecosystem across Europe, opening vital doors with traditional banks and payment service providers.” As a pivotal milestone in this compliance strategy, Gate officially launched its new crypto-asset payment solution for the European market, Gate Pay.

Gate Pay brings together merchant KYB verification, payment settlement, order tracking, refunds, and treasury management in a single environment. The product supports 12 languages, with English as the default alongside other European languages. Its reporting and analytics tools can display amounts in key fiat currencies, including EUR, PLN, and GBP, and USDC is the default settlement currency.

To accommodate both online and offline sales, Gate Pay supports e-commerce and retail scenarios through Static QR Codes. It also offers financial overviews, internal transfers, crypto-to-crypto exchanges, and customer reward distribution, helping merchants manage the process from transaction to treasury. Users can authorise payments via the Gate App or Web Checkout and move funds between their payment account and spot account.

Dr. Giovanni Cunti stated: “Gate Pay is designed to connect European merchants and users with crypto-asset payments within a regulated framework.” He further highlighted: “Strict adherence to rules such as market integrity, transparency, and asset segregation is the true way forward, providing the solid foundation needed for the European market to reach new heights.” Gate will continue to develop its products and risk management practices for the European market.

Learn more about Gate Pay: https://www.gate.com/en-eu/pay

items.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development.
 
The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November.

items.title: Citations vs Promotional Links: 3 Tests to Spot the Difference
items.author: Editing Protocol
items.content:
When fleshing out an article, it’s often necessary to include citations and links to other sources. It’s important for SEO, but it’s also important to show the readers that your claims aren’t being pulled from thin air. However, it’s easy to fall into the trap of including promotional links that bring down the credibility of your article.

If you’re confused about how to differentiate between legitimate citations and promotional links, don’t worry; HackerNoon has you covered. Here are 3 tests to get to the bottom of the truth.

1. The Context Test: Is the link backing up a specific claim, or is it just attached to generic filler text?

Look at the link and where it’s at. If it’s attached to generic text that absolutely needs no backlink, it’s a promotional link. Generic text, in this context, means keyword phrases that are just stuffed into the article for SEO purposes.

When deciding which is the developers usually look for these features.

“Best cloud platform to choose” needs no backlink, and it’s clear that it’s just there to promote a specific cloud platform. Promotional link for sure.

However, if the link is backing up and is attached to a specific claim, then it’s a bona fide citation. Here’s an example:

, 96% of people like to make up statistics on the fly.

It makes sense for the link to be there because you want to cite the place where you got the info from, which, in this case, is RealNews.com.

2. The Swap Test: Could you have linked a neutral source instead?

Think about your source. Was it really necessary for you to pick that one? What happens if you swapped it with a different source? Do things remain the same, or does that drastically change things?

Here’s an example of a promotional link:

, water has a slight blue tint to it

Water is blue is such a generic piece of info that you could’ve used any neutral source. The only reason to use SEOLinkStuffing.com as the source would be to send traffic its way; therefore, it can be considered a promotional link.

Here’s an example of swapping it with a neutral source instead:

, water has a slight blue tint to it.

Same exact claim, but having a neutral source adds more weight to the point you’re trying to make, and it makes your article appear more legitimate.

3. The Destination Test: What will they see when they click the link?

When people click on the link that you put in your article, what will they see? Will they see legitimate info? Or will they be bombarded in the face with promotional content trying to sell them something?

Here’s an example of a bad destination:

You click on the link and immediately get hit with “Book a Demo!”, and you have a ton of branding and marketing for a specific company or tool.

This is not a good look. If people feel as if you wanted them to click on the link just to sell them something, your credibility is instantly destroyed.

Here’s an example of a good destination:

You click on the link, and the only thing the destination website wishes to give you is information. No overly promotional stuff. No Pricing or Services tab in the header.

This is what you want out of a citation. Its only purpose is to back up one of your claims, not to sell you a product.

Use these three tests to figure out whether you’re adding real sources or promotional links to your article and watch your credibility fly through the roof.

items.title: Taming Autonomous AI Agents with Rootless Docker
items.author: Siva Sai Krishna Suryadevara
items.content:
Autonomous coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Cline and their MCP-wired cousins ask before running shell commands by default, but that gate erodes fast in practice. Developers allowlist once, switch on auto-approve for long tasks, or wire an MCP server that calls the Engine API directly with no prompt at all. When agents inherit a Docker CLI pointed at a rootful daemon, every , and socket-mounted sidecar becomes a privileged execution path on the host. Rootless Docker, Linux user namespaces and cgroups v2 together form a containment layer for agent-driven container workloads, provided agents are wired to the right socket and can't fall back to the system daemon.

1. The AI Execution Hazard

The Docker Engine API is root-equivalent. Any process that can open can create a privileged container, bind-mount the host filesystem, or escape through device nodes. Mounting the socket doesn't change this. A read-only bind mount protects the socket file, not the HTTP requests sent through it.

Autonomous agents amplify that blast radius. A single prompt like "reproduce the CI failure in Docker" can cascade into:

  • Unbounded loops that exhaust host memory and inode tables.
  • Nested Docker-in-Docker with , collapsing namespace isolation.
  • Host path mounts () "for debugging," followed by writes outside the workspace.
  • Fork bombs disguised as parallel test runners when is absent.
  • Accidental targeting of production Compose stacks because was never pinned.

The failure mode isn't a malicious operator. It's a probabilistic tool-caller with shell access and incomplete context. A "helpful" retry loop that re-pulls images, recreates networks and restarts Compose projects looks like routine automation in the transcript and like a change storm on the host. The defense has to be structural: demote the daemon itself, then put a quota on every container it creates.

2. Rootless Architecture Under the Hood

Rootless Docker runs and inside a user namespace created by RootlessKit. Every request an agent makes crosses these layers:

[Autonomous agent / MCP server]
              │  Engine API over a user-owned socket
              ▼
[unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock]
              │
              ▼
[Rootless dockerd + RootlessKit]     user, mount and network namespaces; UID remapping
              │
              ▼
[slirp4netns  /  cgroups v2]         user-mode networking; delegated resource controllers
              │
              ▼
[Host kernel, as a non-root UID]     no CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the initial namespace

Subordinate UID/GID mappings

Rootless mode depends on subordinate ID ranges in and :

RootlessKit builds the namespace's ID map from two sources. Container UID 0 maps to the invoking user's own host UID, for example 1001 for . Container UIDs 1 through 65536 map to the subordinate range, so container UID 1 is host UID 100000, and so on.

Root inside a container is therefore never root on the host. A process that escapes a container holds the deploying user's privileges, and files that container root creates on bind mounts are owned by that user. The rule that follows: run agent workloads under a dedicated, low-privilege service account, never a developer's personal login, so that "the user's privileges" means almost nothing.

dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
export DOCKER_HOST="unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock"

starts the daemon under , which creates the namespaces, applies the ID mapping through the setuid helpers and , and starts the networking helper.

Rootful Docker attaches containers to a host bridge () and programs host iptables as real root. Rootless Docker can't. Its network lives inside RootlessKit's own namespace, connected to the host by a user-mode network stack. That's when installed, and otherwise ; is available experimentally. Container traffic leaves the host as ordinary sockets owned by the unprivileged user.

What that means for agent hardening:

  • Any iptables rules the rootless daemon writes live inside RootlessKit's namespace and never touch the host firewall.
  • Publishing host ports below 1024 fails unless you set net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start or grant to .
  • Throughput is lower than with a veth bridge. For agent sandboxes, that trade-off is acceptable.
  • Faster drivers exist, but they widen the trust boundary. needs a setuid binary, and needs a custom seccomp profile. Stay on slirp4netns unless you've measured a need.

Containers egress as the deploying user, not as the host's packet-filter authority. Host firewall policy is therefore a separate concern: don't assume egress restrictions you never configured.

3. Hardening via Linux cgroups v2

User namespaces stop privilege escalation; stops resource exhaustion. Rootless Docker applies cgroup limits only when running with cgroup v2 and systemd. In that case, reports . If it reports , rootless Docker silently ignores , and .

Even with systemd, the user's slice typically receives only the and controllers. and limits require extra delegation, configured system-wide in section 6.

OOM of sibling services, host thrashing

Runaway compile farms stealing cores

Fork bombs from flaky test harnesses

Disk saturation from image pulls and builds

Every agent-launched container should carry explicit limits:

docker run --rm \
  --memory=512m \
  --memory-swap=512m \
  --cpus=1.0 \
  --pids-limit=256 \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m \
  agent-sandbox:latest

Setting equal to disables extra swap. is non-negotiable for agents that spawn shells and package managers. sets a hard quota, while is only a relative weight under contention.

Verify that the CPU controller, the one that usually isn't delegated, actually works:

docker run --rm --cpus=0.5 busybox cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max

You should see . If the command fails or the limit is missing, isn't delegated to your user. Apply the drop-in in section 6 before blaming the agent wrapper.

4. Resolving Agent Sockets

Most agent configurations and MCP servers default to , the system socket. Rootless Docker listens elsewhere:

unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock
typically: unix:///run/user/1000/docker.sock

If is unset and the client falls back to the system socket, every rootless boundary you built is bypassed. Agents running as systemd user units, IDE extensions or MCP child processes often inherit a minimal environment that lacks .

A resolution order that holds up in production:

  1. Honor an explicit .
  2. Else, if $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock exists and is a socket, use it.
  3. Else, fall back to only when policy allows rootful access, and log a loud warning.
  4. Never silently prefer the system socket when a rootless socket is present.

Wrappers and MCP servers should the runtime path before connecting. Pair that with a deny rule if the socket's peer credentials () show UID 0 when the agent expected a user daemon. IDE-spawned children usually inherit but not . Setting explicitly in the MCP server definition matters as much as the rootless install itself.

5. Comparison: Rootful vs Rootless Security Posture

$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock

None (rules stay inside RootlessKit's namespace)

Full host device and kernel access

Capabilities apply only inside the user namespace

Requires systemd driver; / need delegation

Blocked without sysctl or capability changes

Fit for autonomous agents

Rootless isn't a substitute for an application-level policy proxy. It's the execution substrate that makes a compromised or confused agent survivable. Keep the MCP tool surface narrow, and use rootless Docker so whatever still reaches the Engine API can't trivially become host root.

6. Ready-to-Run Artifacts

Place at ~/.config/docker/daemon.json:

{
  "no-new-privileges": true,
  "default-cgroupns-mode": "private",
  "userland-proxy": false,
  "default-ulimits": {
    "nofile": {
      "Name": "nofile",
      "Hard": 4096,
      "Soft": 2048
    }
  },
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  }
}

Containers can't gain privileges through setuid binaries

Each container sees only its own cgroup tree

Lets RootlessKit's port driver propagate client source IPs

Bounds file descriptors per container

Caps log growth from chatty agent jobs

Process limits belong in cgroups through , not in an ulimit. Under user namespaces, counts processes per host UID, so containers would share one budget with each other and with the daemon.

Delegating cgroup controllers (system-wide, once)

Delegation is configured on the system's , not on the user's Docker unit, and needs root:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d

/etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/delegate.conf:

[Service]
Delegate=cpu memory pids io

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
# Log out and back in (or restart user@UID.service), then confirm:
cat "/sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-$(id -u).slice/user@$(id -u).service/cgroup.controllers"

The output should list . Add to the line, which requires systemd 244 or later, if agents need .

User Docker service override

After dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install, cap the daemon itself:

mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user/docker.service.d

~/.config/systemd/user/docker.service.d/override.conf:

[Service]
MemoryMax=2G
CPUQuota=200%
TasksMax=4096

These limits apply to the daemon's own processes: , , RootlessKit and the network helper. Containers get their own systemd scopes, limited per container.

Don't add to this unit. RootlessKit needs the setuid helpers and to build the ID mapping, and stops them from gaining privileges, so the daemon fails to start. Clients choose the socket through , so setting it in this unit has no effect.

systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user restart docker
loginctl enable-linger "$(whoami)"   # keep the user manager running without a login session

Hardened agent container invocation

export DOCKER_HOST="unix://${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/docker.sock"

docker run --rm -i \
  --name "agent-job-${RANDOM}" \
  --memory=512m \
  --memory-swap=512m \
  --cpus=1.0 \
  --pids-limit=256 \
  --cgroupns=private \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --network none \
  --user 65534:65534 \
  alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'echo "contained agent task"; id; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max'

is the right starting point for build and test agents that don't need egress. Open networking only when the task requires it. Dropping all capabilities and running as closes the obvious privilege ladders even inside the user namespace.

Rootless , subordinate ID mappings, user-mode networking and cgroups v2 quotas turn agent container access from an implicit root grant into a bounded, observable workload. The remaining gap is the agent's client side. An MCP server that still resolves quietly undoes all of it.

docker-mcp-guardian is an open-source MCP server that gives Claude and similar agents read-mostly access to Docker. It's read-only by default, resolves restart deny-lists by canonical container name, withholds secrets from inspect output, and bounds every daemon call with a timeout. It also implements the resolution order from section 4: an explicit , then the rootless socket, and the rootful socket only with GUARDIAN_ALLOW_ROOTFUL=true. With no acceptable endpoint it fails closed instead of connecting.

Two open issues take rootless support further, and contributions are welcome:

Pick one, point your own agents at a rootless socket, and help make safe container access the default for autonomous coding tools.
