items.title: Federated AI Still Has a Central Coordinator Problem
items.author: Eepy_engineer
items.content:
Federated Learning Isn’t Decentralized AI (Yet)

Here's the problem federated learning is trying to solve: Most AI training starts with pooling data. That fails wherever the data is sensitive or legally stuck. In 2023, Samsung reportedly restricted employee use of ChatGPT after engineers pasted internal source code into it. In late 2024, Italy’s data protection authority fined OpenAI €15M over how personal data was handled in training. Hospitals hold exactly the data that could improve diagnostic models, but they can’t simply merge patient records.

Federated learning is the standard answer: instead of moving data to the model, move the model to the data. Each site trains locally and sends only model updates to a coordinator, which aggregates them. It’s not theoretical. Google has used it for on-device keyboard prediction in Gboard, and a multi-hospital study (EXAM) trained a COVID-19 oxygen-needs model across roughly 20 institutions without sharing patient records.

“The data never leaves” is not the same as “nothing leaks.” Model updates are computed from private data, and researchers have shown that training examples can sometimes be reconstructed from shared gradients (see Deep Leakage from Gradients, Zhu et al., 2019). Membership inference attacks can also reveal whether a specific record was in the training set.

Real protection needs extra layers:

  • , so the coordinator sees only the sum of updates, not any single site’s contribution.
  • , which adds calibrated noise to updates and gives a measurable privacy guarantee at a cost in accuracy.

Both help. Neither is free. Any claim of “private AI” should come with the accuracy cost attached.

It doesn’t decentralize power

This is the part the marketing skips. In most federated systems, one party runs the coordinator, owns the global model, and decides who participates. The data is distributed, but control isn’t. That’s centralized AI with extra steps.

If the goal is the open, user-owned AI that this contest is about, federation alone doesn’t deliver it. You also need verifiable records of what happened, independent compute, and governance people can contest.

A stack that could actually work

None of this is hypothetical. Each layer has open-source tooling today:

Run training across real, separate machines
Opacus (differential privacy for PyTorch)Add measurable noise to updates
Run client nodes on independent operators, not one cloud vendor
Publish each round’s model hash and training config permanently so anyone can verify provenance
Learn per-site causal graphs locally

The gap nobody talks about: causal structure

Almost all federated learning is about prediction: classify this image, predict the next word. But decisions in medicine and policy depend on causal questions: does this treatment help, or do sicker patients just receive it more often?

Learning causal structure across silos is harder. Sites may measure different variables, confounders differ from site to site, and local graphs may disagree. Federated causal discovery work exists, but it’s far less mature than federated prediction. A practical starting point is to learn a causal graph locally at each site (for example with pgmpy), merge the graphs in an aggregation step, and test whether the merged structure stays consistent across sites.

  • tools like Flower make a federated prototype an afternoon’s work. The hard part is knowing what to measure: the accuracy you lose, the privacy you actually gain, and who runs the coordinator.
  • If you’re a student or researcher: the open problems are at the edges, such as heterogeneous data across sites and causal discovery without pooling records. A small, well-measured experiment there can be a real contribution.
  • If you just use AI products: treat “private AI” as a testable claim. Ask what’s protected, from whom, and at what cost.

A hospital in Delhi, one in Nairobi and one in São Paulo improve a shared model without any patient record leaving the building. The coordinator is a protocol anyone can audit. Every training round leaves a verifiable record of which sources, configuration and model version produced the result. Contributors are rewarded for useful updates instead of having their data harvested for free.

The honest version of this future isn’t “AI owned by everyone.” It’s AI where you can check who trained what, on whose data, under which rules, and where leaving doesn’t mean losing your own contribution. Getting there means solving the dull problems first: measuring the privacy-accuracy tradeoff, handling messy data across sites, and making governance something people can contest.

items.title: How to Generate, Recalculate, and Validate Excel Workbooks With Python
items.author: Malek Damiri
items.content:
The fastest way to lose a finance team is to send them a number they can't click on.

A dashboard shows a total. Finance wants to see how the total was built: which rows, which filter, which formula. If they can't see it, they export the data and rebuild it in Excel, and now there are two numbers and a meeting about why they differ.

So a lot of what I automate for finance ships as a workbook. The detail rows sit on one sheet. The summary cells are formulas that point at them. Click a customer's revenue and you see =SUMIFS(detail!$D$2:$D$7,detail!$B$2:$B$7,A2). Anyone can audit it in the tool they already trust, without asking me a thing.

Generating those workbooks from Python is easy. Generating them so they're actually right takes a few extra steps that nobody mentions until something breaks.

openpyxl writes any string that starts with as a formula. Here's a small revenue workbook: invoices on a detail sheet, and a summary sheet with one per customer, a total, and a check row.

def write_workbook(df, path):
    wb = Workbook()
    detail = wb.active
    detail.title = "detail"
    detail.append(list(df.columns))
    for row in df.itertuples(index=False):
        detail.append(list(row))
    last = len(df) + 1  # header is row 1

    summary = wb.create_sheet("summary", 0)
    summary.append(["customer", "revenue"])
    customers = sorted(df["customer"].unique())
    for i, name in enumerate(customers, start=2):
        summary.append([name, f'=SUMIFS(detail!$D$2:$D${last},detail!$B$2:$B${last},A{i})'])
    total_row = len(customers) + 2
    summary.append(["total", f"=SUM(B2:B{total_row - 1})"])
    summary.append(["check", f"=B{total_row}-SUM(detail!$D$2:$D${last})"])  # must be 0
    summary[f"A{total_row}"].font = Font(bold=True)
    for ws in (summary, detail):
        ws.freeze_panes = "A2"
    wb.save(path)

The check row subtracts the detail total from the summary total. It should always be zero. It's there for the reviewer, and as you'll see, for the code.

Gotcha 1: openpyxl doesn't calculate anything

Open that file in Excel and every formula calculates. Read it with anything else and the formulas have no values:

>>> load_workbook("revenue_2026-09.xlsx", data_only=True)["summary"]["B5"].value
None

pandas does the same thing. A total row written as a formula reads as :

  customer  amount
0     acme  1200.0
1    birch   800.0
2    total     NaN

An xlsx file stores two things for each formula cell: the formula, and the value from the last time it was calculated. openpyxl has no calculation engine, so it writes the first and not the second. Anything that reads values without recalculating, including pandas and the next script in your pipeline, sees nothing.

The fix: let LibreOffice calculate it

LibreOffice can open the file without a window, calculate every formula, and save it back with the values stored:

soffice --headless --calc --convert-to xlsx --outdir out/ revenue_2026-09.xlsx

After that, returns for the total, and the formula is still there for the reviewer. Wrapped in Python:

def recalculate(path, outdir):
    """Open and re-save with LibreOffice so every formula gets a computed value."""
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as profile:  # one profile per process: see below
        subprocess.run(
            ["soffice", f"-env:UserInstallation=file://{profile}", "--headless",
             "--calc", "--convert-to", "xlsx", "--outdir", str(outdir), str(path)],
            check=True, capture_output=True, timeout=120,
        )
    out = Path(outdir) / Path(path).name
    if not out.exists():  # soffice can exit 0 without writing anything
        raise RuntimeError(f"LibreOffice produced no file for {path}")
    return out

Two details in that function exist because of the next gotcha.

Gotcha 2: run six at once and one disappears

If you build several workbooks, the obvious move is to recalculate them in parallel. Here's what happened when I converted six files at the same time with LibreOffice's default settings:

p1 exit=0 p2 exit=0 p3 exit=0 p4 exit=0 p5 exit=0 p6 exit=0 => files: 5

Six processes. Six exit codes of zero. Five files. I ran it again and got the same result.

By default, every LibreOffice process uses the same user profile, and a second that starts while another is running tries to hand its request to the one already running. You can see it in the logs: conversion messages turn up in the wrong process's output. Most requests get done. Sometimes one doesn't, and nothing in the exit code tells you.

The fixes, in order of preference:

  1. -env:UserInstallation=file:///some/unique/dir gives each run its own profile, and they stop interfering. With that change, the same test produced six files out of six. The function above uses a fresh temporary directory for exactly this reason.
  2. Slower, simpler, and what I do for anything that runs unattended.
  3. Check that the output exists, whichever you choose. An exit code of zero from means nothing crashed, not that your file is there. That's the other detail in .

Gotcha 3: newer Excel functions need a prefix

Write =XLOOKUP("b",A2:A3,B2:B3) with openpyxl and Excel shows . So does LibreOffice, which tells you it isn't an Excel quirk:

=XLOOKUP("b",A2:A3,B2:B3)          ->  #NAME?
=_xlfn.XLOOKUP("b",A2:A3,B2:B3)    ->  2

Functions added to Excel after the original file format, such as XLOOKUP, IFS, CONCAT, and TEXTJOIN, are stored in the file with an prefix. Excel adds the prefix when you type the formula. openpyxl doesn't, so you have to.

Gotcha 4, the important one: test the numbers

The workbook exists and the formulas calculate. Are they right? A whose range stops one row short is a perfectly valid formula. So after recalculating, read the values back and compare them with the same totals computed in pandas:

def verify(path, df):
    values = load_workbook(path, data_only=True)["summary"]
    got = {r[0]: r[1] for r in values.iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True)}
    expected = df.groupby("customer")["amount"].sum().round(2).to_dict()
    for name, amount in expected.items():
        assert abs(got[name] - amount) < 0.005, f"{name}: workbook {got[name]} vs data {amount}"
    assert abs(got["check"]) < 0.005, f"check cell is {got['check']}, not 0"
    return got

If any customer is off by more than half a cent, or the check cell isn't zero, the script raises and the workbook doesn't go out. That's the real job of the check row: a reviewer can see it, and the code can enforce it.

before: None
after:  {'Acme': 2260.5, 'Birch': 1775.25, 'Cedar': 300, 'total': 4335.75, 'check': 0}
formula kept: =SUM(B2:B4)

Dashboards are good at "what's happening?" Workbooks are good at "show me." Finance asks the second question far more often, especially at month end, and especially about the numbers that move money.

A workbook with live formulas answers it without a meeting. It also makes your work auditable by the people whose job is auditing, which is the fastest way I know to get them to trust a number they didn't build.

items.title: Grading a Machine That Read 51,008 Pages With No Answer Key
items.author: Vladimir Beskorovainyi
items.content:
Konstantin Tsiolkovsky (1857–1935) derived the rocket equation and described the multistage rocket and the orbital station decades before anyone could build them. His personal papers are held as fond 555 of the Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Moscow. The archive did the essential work years ago: it scanned the fond and put the images online. What it did not provide was a catalogue you can query, full-text search or a dataset. To find anything, you click through page views one file at a time.

Over the summer I built the missing layer: a catalogue of all 2,019 files, a dating for 1,969 of them taken from the archive's own catalogue cards, a classification of every page as handwriting or typescript, and a machine transcription of every page. All of it is public: a full-fond search, the dataset with a permanent DOI (10.5281/zenodo.21705221), the code and the preprint.

One caveat belongs at the top. The machine read everything and no human has verified a single page. The corpus is a finding aid, not a scholarly edition, and every file links back to the archive's own scan, which remains the source of record.

"Digitized" is not "usable"

Three things about the archive's portal only became visible once I tried to use it as a data source.

The identifier in a page address is not the archival file number. Id 300 is file 297, because 31 files carry lettered numbers (145a, 585a and others) that take a position in the running sequence without advancing the archival count. A catalogue built on the obvious reading of the URLs would cite the wrong files.

The inventory number in the address is decorative. Two URLs that differ only in that number return the same document. The real archival address appears only inside the file paths of the scans.

Large scans, above roughly 800 KB, are served cut off at about 130 KB. A browser saves the stub silently with no error. The only way to get them whole was byte-range requests.

None of this is a complaint about the archive, which scanned and published 51,008 pages. It shows the distance between images on the internet and a collection you can ask questions of.

Why model confidence is not a metric

To measure recognition accuracy you need ground truth: the same text keyed in by a person. For an archival fond there is none. If there were, machine reading would be unnecessary.

The usual workaround is to lean on the model's own confidence. It does not work here, and I doubt it works anywhere that matters. A fluent invention satisfies a confidence score as well as a correct reading does. On century-old handwriting, fluent invention is exactly the failure you are worried about.

The answer key the typewriter left behind

Personal archives of the typewriter era often keep one text twice: the author's manuscript and a typescript copy made from it, filed together. I read both with the same pipeline and compare the two transcriptions. The text is the same and the pipeline is the same. The only variable left is how legible the page is, so the disagreement between the two readings measures the difficulty of the handwriting.

Fond 555 holds 1,759 such pairs across 224 files. At the median, the two readings agree on 37% of the words. The median longest run they share verbatim is 10 words, and in 43% of pairs no shared run is longer. That is what "machine-read early twentieth-century manuscript" honestly means.

A proxy metric needs its own validation, and here that was possible in a small corner of the fond: files whose text also survives in a printed edition. On those, the paired-reading estimate is unbiased to within a percentage point of the true error. It also ranks pages by difficulty the way the truth does: a rank correlation of 0.67 across all 55 available pairs, 0.92 on the 32 pairs where the printed edition is demonstrably the same text, and 0.97 on the 17 most certain.

Scored directly against published editions, the transcription reaches 98.1% character accuracy on typescript and 81.1% on handwriting, or 91.7% and 73.7% at word level. Those two figures need a precise label. They were measured on the part of the corpus read by the earlier pipeline. The rest of the fond was read later by a different model and has not been scored against editions. What was measured across both parts is the paired agreement, and it is the same for both. That supports "the newer part reads no worse than the older one". It does not support "81% across the whole fond", and I do not claim it.

This is the rule I would carry into any production system. You almost never have ground truth for everything, but you almost always have it for something. Use that small piece to calibrate a proxy, check that the proxy ranks cases the way the truth does, and only then scale it.

Three results that looked like results

Each of these first looked like a success.

Comparing the author's drafts turned out to be impossible. The fond holds Tsiolkovsky's "The Spaceship" in two variants, ideal material for studying how he revised it, and part of the reason I started. The two variants share 19% of their words. That is below the 37% at which two machine readings of one and the same page agree. Below the noise floor, authorial revision cannot be told apart from reading error. I closed that line of work and built the limit into the tool: the comparison script refuses to report differences that do not clear the measured threshold.

The page classifier passed its test and was still wrong. I separated handwriting from typescript by the variation in ink-stroke lengths along a line. On 19 hand-labelled pages it scored 19 out of 19. Later an independent signal appeared on 4,675 transcribed pages, and against it the classifier is 80% accurate, where always guessing the commoner class gives 54%. Carbon copies and faded typescript read as handwriting. A small, clean test set certifies a demo, not a system.

A model defect posed as data. On 236 pages the model looped and repeated one line of markup, 635 times at worst. Each repeat counted as an uncertainty mark and inflated the published total by 6,189. No statistical check caught it, because 236 pages out of 51,008 do not move any distribution. A person opening a file and looking at it did. The runs are now folded, each with a note on the page saying so, and the corpus carries 299,939 uncertainty marks, about six per scan.

The difference between a measurement and an impression is that a measurement can tell you that you were wrong. Publishing those corrections is what makes the surviving numbers worth trusting.

The truncation that looked like bad reading

Newer models enable reasoning by default, and it draws on the same output budget as the answer. With a 4,096-token limit, up to 3,929 tokens went to reasoning. The transcription broke off mid-page, and the stub was indistinguishable from a poor reading. With reasoning set to minimum, quality did not drop and output volume halved.

If your pipeline evaluates model outputs, a silent truncation upstream will present itself as a quality problem downstream. Check the finish reason before you check the text.

A related edge case: two pages could not be read by any model. They are a German typewritten review of a 1927 Tsiolkovsky pamphlet, and they trip the built-in filter against reproducing known printed text verbatim. They were read by a separate route and are flagged in the corpus.

Choosing the model by measurement, not by price list

I compared candidate models on the same handwritten pages, scored against the typed copy of the same text, with the existing pipeline as the baseline. On typical handwriting no model clearly outran the rest. On a 48-page sample the more expensive model was better on 37 pages and worse on 11. The edge is real but modest, because the ceiling is set by the material, not the model.

The remaining 41,212 pages were read overnight in one batch run, for about $39. The bottleneck in work like this stopped being compute some time ago. It is measurement.

What carries over to production

  • Most systems hold some outputs twice in different forms: a document and its summary, a form and its scan, a query and its report. Agreement between two independent paths is a usable proxy for error.
  • Validate the proxy on the little ground truth you have, and check that it ranks cases correctly, not only that its average is close.
  • Report the noise floor and let it constrain the product. If a difference is below it, the tool should refuse to show it.
  • Distribution-level checks miss rare, loud failures.
  • Truncation masquerades as poor quality.
  • Benchmark on your own material against a baseline before choosing a price tier.

My previous post, The Model Was Never the Bottleneck, ended in the same place from the other side: the work that decides whether an AI system can be trusted is rarely the model itself.

Author’s note: This is an independent project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences. The method is described in a preprint (arXiv:2608.03617); the data are released under CC0 and the code under MIT.

items.title: Blue Origin Announces New Glenn Third Stage, New Booster Engine
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Blue Origin has unveiled a third stage called GS3 for its New Glenn rocket, designed to deliver satellite constellations directly to geostationary orbit and support heavy-lift missions to the Moon and deep space. The company also announced Northstar, a new methalox booster engine that it says produces 715,000 pounds of thrust while cutting mass by 30% and parts by 50% compared with the BE-4. Space.com reports: The new stage will be powered by one BE-7 engine, which the company developed for use on its Blue Moon spacecraft, one of the two private vehicles that NASA selected to be crewed lunar landers for its Artemis program. (The other is SpaceX's Starship.) Blue Moon landing missions won't need to launch on GS3-equipped New Glenn rockets, according to Blue Origin. But the third stage "can support sustained operations around the moon," the company wrote in today's blog post. "By delivering significant payload mass directly to trans-lunar injection (TLI), GS3 enables faster transit times while preserving propellant for on-orbit operations." And there's already demand for such services: Blue Origin also announced today that a government customer (which it did not name) has booked a GS3 mission to cislunar (Earth-moon) space, with launch targeted for 2028.
 
And the company dropped yet more news today -- that it's working on a new first-stage engine, called Northstar. Like Blue Origin's other booster engine, the BE-4, Northstar burns liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant, a combination known as methalox. But the new engine is more powerful and less complex. "Compared to the BE-4 engine, Northstar reduces mass by 30% and parts count by 50%, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force," Blue Origin said in a second blog post today. "Manufacturing advancements have also significantly shortened production timelines, enabling assembly in less than a day." Northstar went from program approval to development testing in just 11 months, according to the company. But today's update did not say when the new engine will fly for the first time.

items.title: Why Robots Need Intelligence Built for the Physical World
items.author: Jon Stojan Journalist
items.content:
Robbyant’s LingBot 2.0 starts with the demands of perception and physical action to build intelligence across different robot bodies.

A chatbot can wait for another prompt. A robot may already be moving by the time its surroundings change. That difference turns embodied AI into a distinct engineering problem, where intelligence has to account for physical space and predict how an action will affect what happens next. , an embodied , built LingBot 2.0 around those demands from the beginning.

The system reflects a deceptively difficult question in robotics: What does an AI architecture need when its decisions have immediate physical consequences? Robbyant’s answer connects perception, environmental modeling, and execution through six models developed as parts of one embodied-native system.

Physical Intelligence Begins With Perception

A robot operating in a home or workplace receives a continuous stream of spatial information. Objects have depth and position, people move around, and the environment can change during a task. Understanding a verbal instruction covers only one piece of that process.

form the perception side of LingBot 2.0. They give robots information about objects and three-dimensional space that can feed into later reasoning and action. Robbyant describes this layer as “See Clearer,” reflecting the need for physical agents to understand where things are before deciding how to interact with them.

That spatial information also has to remain useful as conditions develop. A robot reaching toward an object needs intelligence capable of working with the environment it encounters at that moment.

World Models Give Actions Consequences

The next part of the system addresses prediction. LingBot-Video and LingBot-World 2.0 model physical environments and how they develop over time, creating Robbyant’s “Think Deeper” layer.

This ability has particular significance for robots because movement changes the environment. Picking something up alters its position. Moving through a room creates a new spatial relationship with everything nearby. Effective reasoning involves anticipating what an action is likely to produce.

The models give developers a way to study environmental interaction alongside the perception data that informs it. That relationship is central to Robbyant’s full-stack approach: seeing and predicting supply information that execution can use.

Execution Has to Keep Pace

Eventually, the robot has to move. and LingBot-VA 2.0 handle the “Act Faster” portion of the architecture, translating information from earlier stages into physical behavior.

LingBot-VA 2.0 serves as the capstone of the system. Rather than adapting a model trained for language or entertainment purposes, Robbyant built it from scratch around the demands of embodied AI, with dynamic modeling and causal prediction incorporated into an architecture intended for environmental interaction and real-time execution.Latency becomes especially consequential here. Software generating text can spend additional time producing an answer with few physical consequences. A robot responding to movement around it operates on a different clock. Its perception and reasoning have to reach the action system quickly enough for the response to remain relevant.

One Brain Faces Many Bodies

Hardware creates another complication: bodies differ. A model working on one physical configuration may eventually need to control machines with different dimensions or capabilities.

Robbyant frames its goal as “building one brain for all robots.” LingBot-VLA 2.0 integrates data from 20 different configurations of robots from 17 different brands during the pre-training phase, enabling cross-embodiment capabilities. LingBot 2.0 as a whole approaches that ambition at the system level, connecting specialized capabilities so embodied intelligence can develop across different robot forms. The six-model architecture gives perception, prediction, and action defined roles within the same technical framework.

Selected models and technologies have also been released as open source, accompanied by technical reports or research papers. That gives developers and researchers material they can inspect and reuse while exploring embodied AI architectures.

A Robot Brain Starts With Reality

The technical challenge of embodied AI begins once intelligence has to exist inside physical space. Every decision occurs amid changing surroundings, and an action can immediately create the conditions for the next one.

LingBot 2.0 treats that cycle as a foundation of robot intelligence. Its six models divide the work across seeing, understanding physical change, and executing movement while remaining connected as a full-stack system. For Robbyant, building a more general robot brain starts with understanding what happens when software has to act in the real world.

This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program.

items.title: The $50 Million Gamble That Made Red Bull Marketing History
items.author: yuna
items.content:
Imagine someone asks you, “Hey, do you want to jump from the edge of space?”

Your first response would probably be, “What the hell is wrong with you?”

But when that exact question was asked to , he basically went, “Yeah, sure. Why not?”

Now, you might be wondering who on Earth was crazy enough to ask that question in the first place.

Enter our main protagonist:

Ladies and gentlemen, this is the story of the Red Bull Stratos mission: a man crazy enough to jump from the edge of space, a company crazy enough to fund it, and a PR gamble that somehow paid off spectacularly.

Five Minutes of Marketing So the Rest Makes Sense

Everything you’re about to read comes from me spending the last few hours buried in articles, reports, and marketing resources because apparently that’s what I do for fun now. I tried reading an actual marketing textbook, but it made me question reality, so I fled to Wikipedia, reports, and other resources instead. If I get something wrong, please let me know! Constructive corrections are always welcome—I like learning more than pretending I’m right.

Enough corporate jargon. Let's throw a man out of space.

Now switch the M and the E, and you get —okay, that’s not how names work. You get . But let’s not get distracted.

Earned Media Value (EMV) is the estimated dollar value of publicity a brand receives without paying for it directly.

“The estimated dollar equivalent of unpaid public exposure.”

Which is technically correct, but sounds like a corporate robot wrote it.

So here’s the version my brain understands:

You do something. People can’t stop talking about it. You didn’t pay them to talk about it. That’s EMV.

Influencers posting because they genuinely found something cool? EMV.

People sending the campaign to their friends? EMV.

Throwing a man out of the edge of space?

Yeah... people are definitely going to talk about that.

Spoiler alert: they did. A lot.

So how is EMV calculated?

A simplified formula looks something like this:

EMV = (Total Impressions × Industry CPM) ÷ 1,000

  • = How many times people saw the content.
  • = Cost Per Mille (the cost of reaching one thousand people through advertising).

Basically, it estimates how much money the brand would have had to spend on advertising to achieve the same amount of attention.

Some companies also factor in engagement, audience quality, creator influence, and even audience sentiment. After all, ten million people saying, “This campaign is brilliant,” and ten million people saying, “This campaign is terrible,” are two very different outcomes.

So why do brands care about EMV?

Because it lets them estimate the value of all the buzz they generated without paying directly for every conversation.

Imagine your campaign gets millions of people talking. If buying that same amount of attention through traditional advertising would’ve cost millions of dollars, that’s exactly what EMV is trying to estimate.

One very important thing to remember:

It isn’t money sitting in Red Bull’s bank account.

It’s simply a way of estimating the advertising value of the attention they earned.

Return on Investment (ROI)

Compared to EMV, ROI is wonderfully straightforward.

ROI simply measures how much profit (or loss) you made compared to how much you invested.

ROI = (Net Profit ÷ Cost of Investment) × 100

  • = Money earned − Money spent
  • = Everything you invested into the project

Let’s use a simple example.

Suppose you invest into something.

At the end, you make

ROI = (500 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 50%

That means your investment generated a

A means your investment made money.

A means you lost money.

(Or, as I like to call it, congratulations—you’ve invented a very expensive hobby.)

So what’s the difference between EMV and ROI?

“How valuable was all the attention we earned?”

“Did we actually make money compared to what we spent?”

The other measures financial performance.

We’ll need both of these in a minute because Red Bull Stratos wasn’t just an engineering miracle.

And that's exactly why Red Bull Stratos is still taught as one of the greatest marketing campaigns ever executed.

Somewhere inside Red Bull, on what was probably a completely normal Tuesday, someone had a thought.

A completely normal thought, according to Red Bull standards. Which is already slightly concerning, because Red Bull’s definition of “normal” has historically been questionable.

“Everyone is doing television commercials, right?”

Someone else probably replied:

Then came the question that changed everything:

“What if we didn’t make a commercial?”

“What if we made an event?”

At the time, YouTube livestreaming was still a relatively new idea. Instead of buying a traditional advertising slot, Red Bull could create something people would actively choose to watch.

Something nobody had ever seen before.

What could possibly be big enough to capture the world’s attention?

“What if a man jumped from the stratosphere?”

Now, most companies would probably stop here and call it a concerning brainstorming session.

Red Bull looked at the idea and apparently said:

“Excellent. Let’s do it.”

And just like that, Red Bull Stratos was born.

With an estimated investment of around $50 million, Red Bull wasn’t simply funding a stunt. They were funding a scientific mission, an engineering challenge, and one of the boldest marketing gambles in history.

Fifty million dollars is the kind of money that makes normal people rethink buying a coffee.

Red Bull looked at that amount and thought:

“Perfect. Let’s use it to make a human being fall from the sky.”

Unlike certain Formula 1 teams that shall remain unnamed (Ferrari, I’m looking at you), Red Bull actually had a plan.

And somehow, they executed it.

An Austrian skydiver with years of experience performing extreme jumps, Felix was not exactly someone who looked at a dangerous idea and immediately walked away.

When Red Bull approached him with the idea of jumping from the stratosphere, his reaction was essentially:

Which is either the bravest sentence ever spoken or the sentence responsible for several safety engineers losing sleep.

But this wasn’t just a man standing on a platform and falling.

Behind that jump were scientists, engineers, safety experts, pressure suits, a specially designed capsule, and a massive helium balloon carrying Felix nearly 39 kilometers above Earth.

Basically, hundreds of extremely intelligent people worked together to make sure one person could safely do something that sounded like a rejected cartoon plot.

The Jump That Broke Records

On October 14, 2012, Felix Baumgartner stepped out of his capsule approximately 39 kilometers above Earth.

During his free fall, he reached a maximum speed of around 1,357 km/h, making him the first person to break the sound barrier during a free fall.

The entire event was livestreamed, from the balloon launch to the moment Felix stepped into the unknown.

And that was the genius part.

This was not a commercial people had to sit through before watching something else.

This was the thing people wanted to watch.

The jump itself lasted around 10 minutes, with approximately 4 minutes and 20 seconds spent in free fall before his parachute opened.

What looked like a man simply falling from the sky was actually years of preparation, engineering, testing, and scientific collaboration.

And that was the terrifying part.

Red Bull had spent years preparing for a moment that would last only a few minutes.

But those few minutes had the potential to become one of the greatest marketing successes ever created.

a very expensive, very public disaster.

Because this was not a pre-recorded commercial where a company could quietly delete the footage and pretend nothing happened.

The entire world was watching.

And the internet, famously known for being calm and reasonable during unexpected events, was waiting.

If something went wrong, millions of people would see it happen in real time.

Red Bull wasn’t just risking $50 million.

They were risking their reputation.

They had spent years preparing for a moment that would last only a few minutes.

And then Felix stepped out of the capsule.

Remember That $50 Million?

At no point during the livestream did Felix stop mid-free fall, pull out a can of Red Bull, take a sip, and say,

“Wow. This gives you wings.”

“Look at me! I’m literally flying through the stratosphere!”

Weirdly enough, that wasn’t necessary.

Because he was wearing a Red Bull-branded pressure suit.

The capsule was Red Bull-branded.

The parachute was Red Bull branded.

The massive helium balloon carrying him nearly 39 kilometres into the sky?

They didn’t interrupt people’s attention.

Nobody tuned in because they wanted to watch an advertisement.

They tuned in because they thought,

“Oh my God. Someone is actually going to jump from the edge of space.”

Humans have a fascinating habit of stopping to watch extraordinary things unfold.

A historic sporting moment.

When something unbelievable happens, people naturally gather around it.

Red Bull understood that psychology.

Instead of asking millions of people to spend thirty seconds watching their advertisement...

...they created something millions of people willingly spent hours watching.

And the brand just happened to own that moment.

Because Red Bull has never really sold caffeine.

They’ve sold the idea that normal is boring.

People don’t buy Red Bull because it’s simply an energy drink.

They buy into everything the brand represents.

Whether that’s Formula 1, cliff diving, mountain biking, air races, or a man casually deciding gravity is optional.

Then the internet did what the internet does best.

Teachers showing it in classrooms.

Friends sending each other the livestream.

Every conversation became free advertising.

Exactly what we talked about earlier with Earned Media Value.

The numbers speak for themselves.

Nearly eight million people watched simultaneously on YouTube.

Hundreds of millions watched clips afterwards.

The campaign generated an estimated in earned media value.

And perhaps most importantly...

Everyone remembered who made it happen.

Red Bull didn’t interrupt millions of people to tell them they were exciting.

They did something so exciting that millions of people interrupted their own lives to watch.

Sometimes the best advertisement...

...isn’t an advertisement at all.

items.title: The Zero-Budget AI Launch Playbook: 80% of Your Launch Happens Before Launch Day
items.author: Elsa
items.content:
Part 1 of 2: How to earn attention from Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt when you have no ad budget

  • In the AI era, ideas and even whole products get cloned in a weekend. Distribution is the part AI can't copy for you.
  • A launch is not a day. By the time you hit "publish," about 80% of the work should already be done.
  • One rule beats every tactic: give value before you take value.
  • On Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt, patience and reputation beat polish and hype. Fast, promotional launches get removed, banned or ignored.
  • You can build your first real audience for roughly zero dollars if you create something useful your product before the product exists.

Your idea is not the moat. Distribution is.

Try this thought experiment. You have a good idea for an AI product. How long before someone else ships something nearly identical?

A year ago the honest answer was a few months. Today, with Claude Code, Cursor and a dozen other tools, it's closer to a long weekend. You can polish the model, sand down the UX, tune the prompts. Competitors can do all of that too, and they'll do it faster than you'd like.

What they can't copy overnight is who already knows you exist: the communities that trust you, the search results that surface you, the people who will say your name when someone asks "what should I use for this?" That's distribution, and it's still stubbornly human work.

I come from a growth background and have worked on go-to-market for several AI products: a music generator, an AI companion app, a financial-data platform, and a few others. I've done launches with money and without it. Some of them worked. Some of them got my accounts banned. This two-part series is the playbook I wish I'd had at the start, with the failures left in.

Part 1 is about the launch itself and the three communities most founders obsess over: Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt. Part 2 covers search, PR, creators and the art of making noise.

Launch day is the last 20%

When I picture "launching a product," my brain reaches for the standard toolkit: buy promotion, record a slick demo video, line up a wave of creators to post the same demo on the same day with the same script, and manufacture the feeling that this thing is blowing up.

That's a valid playbook, and I'll get to it. But it hides the most important fact about launches: the visible event is the tip of the iceberg.

Take Product Hunt. Whether your product climbs the daily ranking has very little to do with what you do that day. It depends on whether, months earlier, you quietly gathered people who care. We live in an attention economy where everyone is distracted by something else, so the traffic and noise you capture on launch day are a function of the groundwork underneath.

The same goes for offline. A great launch is rarely purely online. It leans on the founder friends you met at a conference, the developers you traded favors with, the investor who happily retweets your news. These threads connect to each other, and none of them can be pulled out of thin air the week before.

So the first reframe: stop asking "how do I launch?" and start asking "what can I build in the 90 days before the launch that makes launch day easy?"

The one rule: give value before you take value

If I could only give you one principle, it would be this: share the value, not your product.

In marketing terms: give first, collect later. Put something genuinely useful in front of people before you ask for anything. Don't expect anyone to use your product in return. They have alternatives, they owe you nothing, and they can smell an agenda from the first sentence.

I'll keep returning to this idea, because it shows up everywhere: in how you post on Reddit, how you write comments, how you build an audience, how you approach creators, even how you make friends at conferences. The tactics change by channel. The rule doesn't.

It also changes how fast you should move. Value-first marketing is slow by design. If you're in a hurry, you'll be tempted to skip straight to the ask, and the channels below are very good at punishing that.

Product Hunt: a ranking, not a strategy

Product Hunt is where most founders start, so let's be honest about what it has become.

The best example I know of a Product Hunt launch is Gamma, the AI presentation tool. As I remember it, they spent a long time building up a large group of loyal early users before they launched, back when Product Hunt's credibility was still intact. On launch day they rallied those users, and the upvotes were real: actual customers vouching for a product they already liked. That's the model. The ranking was the of earlier work, not a substitute for it.

Today the picture is murkier, for three reasons:

  • Some well-known hunters will, for a fee, endorse your product or help push it up the list. Founders also blast every group chat they're in, begging friends to upvote. A #1 spot on the daily chart may mean the product is great. It may also mean the founder had the best hustle.
  • If several products launch on the same day, you can get lost in the pile. Pick a quieter day.
  • My honest view is that, for most teams, Product Hunt is no longer a high-ROI launch channel. The effort to climb the chart often outweighs the customers it brings.

My suggestion: treat Product Hunt as an optional credibility badge, not your launch. If you already have a base of users who will show up and vouch for you organically, go for it, and choose a calm day. If you don't, spend those weeks building the base.

Hacker News: earn your seat, then be interesting

My team and I have launched on both Product Hunt and Hacker News, and I find Hacker News the more community-driven of the two. It's run by Y Combinator, and it is famously hard to game. If you're thinking about creating a stack of accounts to push a post up the front page, don't bother.

Three things I'd tell anyone planning a Hacker News post:

1. Start building your account months ahead. If you want to share an article or a launch there someday, begin now. Spend three or four months commenting thoughtfully on other people's posts and becoming a recognizable voice. You can't suddenly decide on launch week to do something promotional. The community leans technical and pure, and it reacts badly to anything that smells like marketing.

2. Reputation is what keeps a post alive. If you've made real friends in the community and respected regulars comment on your post, it stays visible far longer. Without that, it sinks quickly.

3. Interesting beats technical. You don't need to publish hardcore engineering to get noticed. When we were working on an AI music product, ChatGPT went down one day. We wrote a song about the outage and shared it. It caught fire on Hacker News, a small but very real win. The bonus came afterwards: a number of people who write technical blogs saw it and linked to our song from their own posts, which handed us several natural backlinks for free.

That last part is worth sitting with. We didn't set out to win backlinks. We made something people wanted to share, and the SEO benefit came as a by-product. That's value-first marketing in miniature.

Reddit: three plays that work (and the one that got my accounts banned)

If you have a small budget or none at all, Reddit is the channel I'd look at first, but only if you can start two to three months early to build up karma and a credible profile.

One warning before the tactics: don't outsource your posts to someone else's accounts. Only the founder really knows what the product feels like, and many "we'll post for you" accounts just generate generic AI-written content that readers sniff out immediately.

Play 1: Comparison posts, in small subreddits

Write a genuine comparison of your product and similar tools. Be fair. Cover the pros cons of your competitors as well as your own, and write as a user of AI tools rather than as the company.

Then post it in with a few hundred to a few thousand members, ideally ones whose rules aren't strict about self-promotion. Avoid the giant communities. Their moderators have seen every flavor of disguised promotion and will remove it.

Why bother if the audience is tiny? Because the goal isn't Reddit traffic. It's two long-tail effects:

  • Reddit ranks well on Google, often in the top five for searches that include a product name. A comparison thread can outrank the same comparison on your own blog.
  • Credibility for people who are already curious. Someone hears about your product, isn't sure whether to download it, and searches "your product + reddit" to see what real people think. Having a fair, readable thread there helps.

The mistake people make is wanting both: a comparison post thousands of eyeballs, so they post it in a huge subreddit and get it removed. Pick one goal.

Posts are slow and risky. Comments are underrated.

  1. List the questions your target users ask, especially the ones tied to a real pain your product solves.
  2. Watch for new threads asking those questions, ideally within the last 24 to 48 hours, and the fresher the better.
  3. Reply as a helpful community member: "there are a few ways to approach this. First, ... second, ..." Leave out the link.

This only works if your profile looks like a real community member's and not a billboard. Participate in discussions that have nothing to do with your product.

Play 3: Posts that share value, not products

If you do want to post, make it beneficial to others first. In my experience, the posts that have done well for me, reaching tens of thousands of views and thousands of upvotes, all shared something useful and weren't ads.

Building an AI music product? Share your favorite playlists, artists or recent releases in the right music community. Building an AI travel product? Share routes. Weaving your product into a post in a natural way is , so don't force it.

And here's the pattern that works: Post the same kind of thing on a schedule, say one or two playlists a week. For the first four weeks, mention nothing about your product. Let people get used to you as the person who brings good music. Only when the community knows you can you say, "By the way, I'm building this, and it tries to solve that." By then it feels like a friend sharing news.

Reddit communities care deeply about their atmosphere. If people recognize you as someone who adds value, they upvote you and thank you in the comments. If not, you're gone.

The lesson is the one I started with: you can't extract value from a community before you've put some in.

Build the audience before the product

The cheapest launch I've ever run started months before there was a product to launch.

We were building a data platform, something like a Bloomberg-style terminal where people can explore all kinds of data. The question every founder in that position asks is: where do the first users come from?

My answer was to build a media publication with the product. While the platform was being developed, the publication used its data to write analysis: price trends, macroeconomic outlooks, that kind of thing. Readers found the articles useful enough to forward to friends, and they spread well in several markets. At the bottom of each piece, we invited readers into a private community (a Discord server, for readers outside China).

Then the loop did its work:

  1. based on the product's data prove the data is valuable, without sounding like an ad.
  2. collects the readers who care, in a place we own.
  3. comes next. Readers of the analysis naturally wonder whether they can see the raw data and draw their own conclusions. Now they can, with invite codes and referral mechanics that encourage a second wave of sharing.
  4. arrives last. By now the community has hundreds of engaged people who know the product and are happy to help you launch it.

The whole thing cost almost nothing. It worked because the content and the product were tightly connected: the articles were the product's data, so every reader was already a qualified prospect.

If you take one idea from this section, take this: find the valuable thing your product makes possible and give that away publicly, long before you ask for a signup.

A 90-day pre-launch checklist

  • Months 3 to 2 before launch: Create or revive your Reddit and Hacker News accounts. Comment daily on threads where you can genuinely help. Pick two or three small subreddits to become a regular in.
  • Start a recurring, value-only post series in one community. Publish content built from your product's insight or data. Begin collecting an email list or private community.
  • Write your comparison posts. Open a small beta with invite codes. Quietly line up the supportive people (users, friends, fellow founders) who will show up on launch day.
  • Choose a quiet day if you use Product Hunt. Post where you've earned the right to. Reply to every comment.
  • Share value first. Never buy upvotes, farm karma or cross-vote your own accounts.

Everyone wants the shortcut: the viral post, the front-page ranking, the one tweet that changes everything. Sometimes shortcuts exist. But the launches that hold up are the ones that look like overnight successes and turn out to be slow, boring groundwork on the inside.

Give first. Be patient. Show up in the places where your users already are, as one of them.

In , I'll cover the other half of the playbook: starting SEO on day one with long-tail keywords, using PR to build authority (including with AI search), working with creators without wasting money, and what to make of the rising wave of attention-grabbing stunts, including the cautionary side of the story.

items.title: Google's 2027 LSA Expansion Has an API Availability Problem
items.author: Mayur S
items.content:
Google's planned 2027 expansion of Local Services Ads (LSAs) creates an important technical question for agencies and software providers: will Google Ads API capabilities expand at the same pace as the advertiser migration?

Google's migration roadmap says non-US accounts and remaining business categories will transition to Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals in 2027. Yet the current Google Ads API documentation still restricts the field for these campaigns to .

This is not proof that international API support will arrive late. Google may update its API documentation and regional capabilities before the relevant migration phases begin. But it exposes an integration risk that agencies should address before international accounts move into the new campaign architecture.

The issue is bigger than campaign creation. It affects account provisioning, location validation, campaign automation, conversion-goal configuration, reporting, and the ability to manage multiple markets through a single software layer.

The migration roadmap and API documentation are not at the same stage

Google is moving LSAs into a specialized Performance Max campaign structure while retaining the pay-per-lead model and local placements on Search and Maps.

Its published migration schedule has three broad phases:

August 2026: selected US home and storefront services

Late 2026: broader advertiser groups, including service-area businesses and professional services

2027: non-US accounts and remaining supported categories

The API documentation describes a more limited geographic capability at present. The Performance Max for pay-per-lead setup requires a two-letter country code in local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.country_code, and the documented supported value is . The documentation also states that location criteria must belong to the campaign's home country.

That creates a distinction between two forms of availability:

  • Product availability: An advertiser can use the pay-per-lead campaign experience in a particular market.
  • API availability: A developer or agency can create, configure, and manage that campaign programmatically in that market.

These capabilities are related, but they are not interchangeable. A campaign becoming available in the Google Ads interface does not automatically establish that every API workflow, field, validation rule, or regional dependency is available too.

The country code is a provisioning constraint, not a cosmetic field

Consider an agency managing campaigns for plumbing businesses in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

A conventional campaign-management platform might represent each account using a shared configuration:

{
  "business_id": "client_104",
  "market": "GB",
  "country_code": "GB",
  "business_profile_id": "123456789",
  "campaign_type": "LOCAL_SERVICES_PMAX",
  "lead_goal": "PHONE_CALL_LEAD"
}

This is a simplified internal representation, not a Google API request.

The problem emerges when the provisioning service translates that configuration into Google's campaign resource. If the API validates the country code against the currently supported value of , an international campaign cannot simply be created by substituting or .

The integration must distinguish between a market supported by the advertising product and one supported by the API provisioning workflow.

A robust system should therefore maintain a capability registry rather than assuming that every market supports every operation.

{
  "market": "GB",
  "product_available": false,
  "api_campaign_creation": false,
  "api_campaign_updates": false,
  "location_targeting": "UNCONFIRMED",
  "last_verified": "2026-11-05"
}

The values above are illustrative. They should be populated from verified Google documentation and account-level eligibility checks, not treated as Google's published UK capability status.

This registry becomes particularly important during phased rollouts. Different accounts may become eligible at different times, even when they operate in the same country or vertical.

API version support does not eliminate regional restrictions

Google's API implementation has also evolved across versions.

The Local Services campaign documentation distinguishes standalone campaigns using:

advertising_channel_type = LOCAL_SERVICES

from Local Services campaigns represented as specialized Performance Max campaigns:

advertising_channel_type = PERFORMANCE_MAX
campaign.pmax_campaign_settings.local_services_enabled = true

This distinction matters for integrations that identify campaigns by advertising channel type alone.

This is part of a broader API transition problem in Google's LSA migration. As I discussed in The Hidden API Problem in Google's LSA-to-PMax Migration, changes to campaign architecture can create compatibility challenges for agencies that depend on programmatic account management. The 2027 international expansion adds another dimension: regional API availability.

Google's documentation now describes Local Services Performance Max campaign creation and management through the API starting in version . Earlier API versions had more limited support, including update-only workflows for eligible campaigns created through the Google Ads interface.

However, API version support and geographic eligibility are separate constraints. Supporting the required resource fields in does not mean every country can use them.

An integration can therefore pass its API-version checks and still fail during campaign creation because a required country, listing, location asset, or account prerequisite is unsupported.

Google Business Profile adds another dependency

Local Services Performance Max campaigns are not configured independently of business-location data.

The API workflow requires a Google Business Profile listing ID through local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.listing_id. Google validates this listing during campaign creation against the associated location assets.

This creates a dependency chain:

  1. The business has an eligible Google Business Profile.
  2. The listing is accessible through the connected Google Ads account.
  3. The required location assets are available.
  4. The campaign references the correct listing ID.
  5. The service-area targeting satisfies the campaign's geographic restrictions.

An international rollout may require more than accepting a new country code. It may also require market-specific validation rules, supported location criteria, phone-number formats, language constraints, and business-verification workflows.

For agencies, this means a campaign provisioning system should not treat a Google Business Profile listing ID as a globally interchangeable identifier. It must validate the relationship between the listing, the account, the market, and the campaign before submitting a mutation request.

Conversion goals create another layer of integration risk

Local Services Performance Max campaigns use a constrained set of lead conversion categories.

The current API documentation identifies:

  • , for eligible POS coupon partner campaigns

For non-coupon campaigns, phone-call leads are automatically configured as the required active goal. Message leads are created but disabled by default. Booking goals depend on an approved Reserve with Google partner being detected on the linked location.

These rules matter because an agency cannot safely assume that a campaign's conversion configuration is identical across every market or account.

A provisioning service should validate the goals returned by the API rather than assuming that a successful campaign creation request means every intended lead channel is active.

It should also separate campaign configuration from actual lead availability. A goal being technically configurable does not guarantee that the underlying service or partner integration is available in a particular market.

What agencies should build before the 2027 rollout

The practical response is to make campaign automation capability-aware.

A single global provisioning workflow is attractive, but it can become fragile when product eligibility, API support, and verification requirements change independently.

A more resilient architecture should include five components:

1. Regional capability registry

Maintain a market-level record of supported campaign operations, API versions, verticals, conversion goals, and location requirements. Store the source and date of each capability check.

Before creating a campaign, validate the account's market, business category, Google Business Profile listing, location assets, and required lead goals. Reject unsupported combinations before sending a mutation request.

3. Version-aware API adapter

Keep Google API resource mapping separate from internal campaign models. This makes it easier to handle changes to resource fields, validation rules, and API versions without rewriting the entire agency platform.

4. Idempotent provisioning

Use an internal provisioning state machine to prevent duplicate campaign creation when requests time out or return ambiguous errors. Record the Google resource name and mutation result before retrying.

5. Regional observability

Track API errors by country, API version, operation, campaign type, and error code. A rise in INVALID_LOCAL_SERVICES_PERFORMANCE_MAX_LISTING_ID errors, for example, should be investigated separately from country-code validation failures.

These controls also make it easier to identify whether a failure comes from account eligibility, API capability, location configuration, or a temporary service issue.

The real 2027 risk is assuming that product rollout equals API readiness

Google's 2027 LSA expansion is a significant platform change, but the most important engineering challenge may be hidden from advertisers. Agencies that depend on API-driven reporting, campaign provisioning, and multi-market automation need to prepare for regional capability differences.

The current documentation establishes a clear constraint: the documented pay-per-lead API workflow is US-specific, while Google's migration roadmap schedules non-US accounts for 2027. Whether those capabilities converge before international migration begins remains something agencies must monitor.

The safest approach is not to build international automation around an assumed rollout date. It is to build systems that can detect regional capabilities, validate account eligibility, and adapt when Google releases new API support.

A global advertising product needs more than a global migration announcement. It needs a globally consistent and documented integration surface.

items.title: “Move Fast and Break Things” Is Dead. What Counts in Enterprise AI Now?
items.author: Victoria Loskutova
items.content:
The invoices are ending Silicon Valley’s favorite motto that built the AI boom.

Right before Facebook went public, Mark Zuckerberg shared the “move fast and break things” motto in his 2012 letter to investors. The idea was to build and launch quickly, fix problems later, and learn from mistakes. Startups across Silicon Valley embraced this approach. During the web and mobile boom, the focus was on gaining users first, with monetization, compliance, and governance left for later. When ChatGPT entered the market, the industry repeated this strategy on a larger scale. Companies scrambled for computing power and began spending heavily on licenses, pilots, and APIs, treating AI as a land grab.

At Facebook’s developer conference in April 2014, Zuckerberg joked about a new motto: “move fast with stable infra.” With 1.28 billion users, breaking things had become expensive.

The motto worked until mistakes became more expensive because of the token costs, and the results stopped matching expectations. In a PwC survey of 4,454 CEOs, 56% said they had seen no significant financial benefit from AI so far.

Costs have also been harder to predict than anyone planned. A Harness study found that 72% of organizations had had an unexpected AI cost spike, and more than half said no one clearly owns AI spending. Harness sells AI cost-management software, so it has a stake in how big the problem looks. Cloudera’s research points to another problem: segmented data systems and silos make it hard for companies to measure what AI really costs them to run.

Then the CFOs Reached for the Cap

In April, Uber’s CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga said the company had used up its entire 2026 AI budget after just four months of Claude Code. Teams had been ranked on an internal leaderboard by how much AI they used. By June, the company limited each employee to $1,500 a month per AI coding tool. In August, Naga wrote that Uber was coming to the end of the so-called “tokenmaxxing era,” when burning tokens meant productivity.

Gartner's advice to CFOs is to treat AI cost as an architecture issue rather than a budget line item. One unmonitored prompt library alone can "risk running up millions of dollars in additional expense".

That’s the new rule. Finance asks the question nobody asked loudly in 2023: what did we get?

How the Ledger Rewrites the Stack

Finance teams can't parse a transformer model, but they can easily understand a unit price. Unit price is now the driver of architecture decisions. So how do you deal with that?

Route tasks wisely. Don’t just send every job to the largest model. In his annual letter on October 21, 2026, Satya Nadella introduced the “cost-to-outcome” frontier: “After all, Super Intelligence is changing every organization’s inputs (how they work) as well as their outputs (the products and services they sell). At the same time, inference is making marginal cost an important factor in software economics as usage scales. As a result, customers will increasingly measure the cost of tokens against the outcomes they produce. We call this the “cost-to-outcome” frontier, and we are focused on optimizing it.”

For engineers, that means sending classification, extraction, and summarisation to a smaller, cheaper model, caching repeated prompts, and using the frontier model only for the work that needs it.

Count everything. FinOps for AI is the top priority in the State of FinOps 2026 Report, and AI expense management is a skill teams currently need to build. In practice, that means tagging every model call by team and feature and giving each agent its own budget and alert, so a runaway loop triggers an alarm before it reaches the invoice.

A new software market is emerging to meet this demand. Max Gontar, CEO of the AI-powered finance software company Kairos, explains:

The first wave of enterprise AI was all about wild spending on experiments in the hope of seeing what the models could write/generate. The current state is that CFOs are getting what they actually need: software that runs within their existing infrastructure to find working capital leaks, deliver tangible ROI and automate finance workflows as a result (that's where AI really is good at). The new challenge for the CFO is the management of AI infrastructure spend. They now have to work out how many tokens it makes sense to spend on each process, what to cut and what to rebuild. The ROI of every function in the business will be more transparent than it's ever been.

Watch who owns the numbers. In the FinOps Foundation’s 2026 survey of 1,192 practitioners, 78% of FinOps teams report to the CTO or CIO, and only 8% report to the CFO. So finance didn’t take control, but it did get veto power. The CFO asks, “What did this return?” and engineering manages the dashboard with the answer.

Balance Sheets vs. the Spark

There’s a problem, though. If every task has to meet a cost limit, who pays for work you can’t predict? Cost-to-serve metrics reward what’s measurable now, but exploration usually isn’t measurable in the short term.

There's no 2026 data at all to show that cost discipline is in any way reducing the amount of exploratory research so it's a valid concern rather than a fact. The moral guidelines, the risk frameworks, the ethical manifestos all sit in a PDF somewhere and are presumably being read. A runaway agent loop doesn't do that. It shows up as a number on a bill and numbers get attention. The ledger will only protect what it can count.

But Big Tech Is Spending More Than Ever

Here's the obvious objection: if the era is over why are the giants still throwing money at it? Forbes has the four biggest spenders (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet) at $700-$725bn of capital expenditure in 2026, up 75% on $410bn in 2025.

This only makes the argument clearer. The sellers are the hyperscalers. They build capacity and fund it with huge cash flows, betting on future demand. Their customers are the buyers, and buyers pay attention to invoices. If a buyer cuts back, chooses cheaper models, or limits usage, it affects the demand that sellers are counting on.

There's a bit of a tension there. Capacity is being built on the basis that the enterprises will be spending a lot more, whilst the same enterprises are in fact capping their usage, moving to cheaper models and asking what they got for the money. One side of that equation is either completely wrong or just way ahead of its time.

Facebook abandoned 'move fast and break things' when it started to get expensive. A decade on and enterprise AI is running into the same wall, just with a much bigger bill. It's not over yet. Finance has the veto, they just can't yet see what they're giving up in terms of accuracy and ambition. 'Move fast and break things' died because of the invoices. The next battle is over what gets counted.

items.title: Learjet Crash Has Brought The Conspiracy Crowd Out of The Woodwork
items.author: Matthew - Technology News Australia
items.content:
Apparently, it was a missile, the government was involved, and the lack of easily recognisable aircraft parts on the ground proves something sinister happened.

Then came the YouTubers comparing the wreckage to the September 11 attack on the Pentagon and the lack of visible aircraft parts, as though putting two crash videos beside each other amounts to an investigation.

These are the kinds of statements I’ve been reading on social media following the Learjet crash in Florida, and the confidence behind them is extraordinary.

Fly-by-night conspiracy theorists have been announcing their conclusions while investigators are still recovering evidence.

People who appear to have little understanding of aviation are presenting themselves as authorities on aircraft structures, impact damage and the circumstances of the crash.

I’ve been around aviation my entire life, and watching this nonsense circulate is infuriating. Someone sees footage they don’t understand, decides the wreckage looks wrong and immeditely starts suggesting a government opration.

The Pentagon comparisons are particularly tiresome. Comparing the appearance of two crash sites cannot establish what happened at either one without examining the aircraft, impact conditions, structures and physical evidence.

Yet these videos invite viewers to treat their own unfamiliarity with aircraft accidents as proof that something has been concealed.

What makes this behaviour so callous is that real people died. They had families and futures, including a 20-year-old pilot whose aviation career had barely begun.

Imagine losing someone you love, then opening social media to find strangers using their final moments to promote an unsupported missile theory.

The aircraft was a Learjet 60, registered N722BD, flying from Austin towards the Bahamas. Flight tracking information and cockpit transmissions document a weather encounter followed by a catastrophic descent near West Palm Beach on 1 November.

The crew reported icing, turbulence and precipitation before reporting an overspeed condition during the descent.

There is meaningful information to examine, but apparently that requires more effort than typing “government cover-up” beneath a video.

My own assessment, based on the information available, is that this looks like poor navigation and possible pilot error during a dangerous weather encounter. That remains my interpretation, subject to the investigation establishing what happened.

The sequence I consider plausible is that icing contributed to an aerodynamic stall and loss of control, followed by a rapidly accelerating descent and structural damage.

Ice forming on the wings, including around their leading edges, can disrupt airflow, reduce lift and increase stall speed. The FAA describes these effects in its guidance on airframe icing.

If sufficient ice accumulated on this aircraft, it could have contributed to a stall and the subsequent nose-down descent.

Investigators will need to establish whether that occurred, how the ice protection systems were operating and what other factors affected the aircraft.

At the reported altitude, temperatures around minus 40 degrees Celsius are conceivable, although altitude alone cannot establish the actual outside air temperature.

Extreme cold also needs to be understood properly: conventional airframe icing depends on supercooled liquid water, which approaches its theoretical freezing limit around minus 40 degrees Celsius.

The crew’s reported icing encounter deserves serious examination. It doesn’t give any of us permission to declare the complete accident sequence proven.

During the extreme descent, increasing speed and aerodynamic loads may have caused part of the tail to separate. Losing an essential pitch control surface would make recovery impossible, depending on the damage and the aircraft’s condition.

Investigators recovered three pieces of the left elevator between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the impact site. They have yet to establish whether its separation contributed to the initial loss of control or resulted from forces acting on the aircraft during the descent.

That is a serious question involving physical evidence. It deserves considerably more attention than someone’s unsupported claim about a missile.

Then there’s the supposedly devastating observation that you “can’t see any aircraft parts on the ground”.

What exactly were these people expecting to see? A smashed up fuselage beside the road, complete with wings and a registration conveniently facing the camera?

Given the aircraft’s mass and impact speed, extensive fragmentation is a credible explanation for why little in the footage resembled a recognisable aircraft.

A violent impact can break an aircraft into small pieces, with wreckage scattered, buried or damaged by fire.

An aircraft striking the ground at close to the speed of sound would carry enormous kinetic energy because of its mass and velocity, potentially comparable to several tonnes of TNT. The impact could reduce much of it to tiny fragments, leaving little recognisable as an aircraft, being effectively “atomised”.

The recovery of aircraft components already undermines the assertion that there was no plane. Failing to identify wreckage in a video says little about what investigators can recover from the scene.

What amazes me is how quickly a lack of knowledge becomes absolute certainty. Someone doesn’t understand the wreckage, so the wreckage must be suspicious. A detail is missing from an early report, so someone must be hiding it.

These people then demand that everyone else disprove whatever they’ve imagined.

I’m prepared to explain what I consider plausible and acknowledge where the evidence remains incomplete. If the investigation establishes a different cause, my assessment will have to change.

Anyone alleging a missile strike or government involvement should bring evidence capable of supporting that accusation. A YouTube comparison with the Pentagon and a comment about missing wings won’t do it.

Nine people died, and their families are now living with that loss. Before posting another smug declaration about what “really happened”, perhaps these self-appointed investigators should consider whether they would repeat it while standing in front of those families.

items.title: Why SSH Still Matters After More Than 30 Years
items.author: Igor Lopushko
items.content:
Imagine managing a server located thousands of miles away. You need to update its software, investigate an application failure, or change a configuration file. You cannot physically access the machine, but you still need to work with it almost as if it were sitting on your desk.

Today, this is a completely ordinary task. Engineers connect to remote servers, execute commands, transfer files, and maintain infrastructure from practically anywhere in the world. Much of this is possible because of a technology called .

SSH is one of those technologies that most people outside the IT industry have probably never heard of, even though it plays an important role in the systems they use every day. Websites, banking platforms, cloud applications, and enterprise services all depend on infrastructure that is frequently managed through SSH.

What makes SSH particularly interesting is its longevity. The protocol was introduced in 1995, when the internet was a very different place. Yet, more than three decades later, SSH remains an essential tool for software developers, system administrators, DevOps engineers, and security professionals.

To understand why it has survived for so long, it is worth looking at the problem it was originally designed to solve, how its security mechanisms work, and how its role has changed as computing has evolved.

What Is SSH, and Why Is It Important?

At its simplest, SSH is a network protocol that allows two computers to communicate securely over a potentially untrusted network. The most familiar use case is remote terminal access. A user opens a terminal, connects to another computer, and begins executing commands.

This command asks the SSH client to connect to a remote machine at the specified IP address using the username . If authentication succeeds, the user can work with the remote system through a command-line session. But SSH is much more than a remote terminal protocol. It can also transfer files, execute individual commands, carry application traffic through encrypted tunnels, and provide secure authentication for automated processes.

The importance of SSH comes from three fundamental security properties:

means that network traffic is encrypted so that someone intercepting the communication cannot easily read its contents.

means that the receiving system can detect unauthorized changes to transmitted data. An attacker should not be able to modify commands or responses without the modification being detected.

helps establish that the client is communicating with the intended server and that the user attempting to access the server has appropriate credentials.
