However, Tailscale clients are Open Source, and Headscale is a self-hosted implementation of the coordination server that the official macOS, iOS, and Synology clients can log into. If I ever want out, I can move my four devices in an afternoon. It's a real exit, albeit not a completely free one: every device gets a new key, a new address, and a new name, and relayed traffic still goes through Tailscale's servers unless I run my own. For now, convenience wins.

The topology is a star. The NAS is always on, so every other device pairs with it only. The laptop, the iPhone, and the iPad never talk to each other. It makes the configuration simpler, at the cost of a single point of failure. I'll get back to it. The NAS has no special role in the protocol. It's the hub only because it never sleeps.

The following assumes Tailscale already runs on every device and that MagicDNS is enabled, so that each device has a name of the form <device>.<tailnet>.ts.net.

Syncthing is available for Synology via SynoCommunity. In the Package Center, add https://packages.synocommunity.com as a package source, then install Syncthing. The package isn't verified by Synology, but it's expected. Once started, the web interface is at http://nas.<tailnet>.ts.net:8384. It has no password by default. Set one under . The package runs under its own user; give it write access to the shared folder in Control Panel.

Open it, then go to Actions > Settings > Connections. Uncheck , , and .

Local discovery is harmless, but I unchecked it too. The NAS doesn't need to find any other devices; devices find it. With NAT traversal on, Syncthing asks the router to forward port 22000 from the Internet, and queries public STUN servers to learn its public address. My router ignores the request, so no port ever opens.

The phone still listed my public IP among the NAS's addresses: the discovery server fills it in from wherever the announcement came from. I unchecked the box anyway, so the NAS talks to neither the router nor the STUN servers.

Syncthing connections work in both directions, so it's enough for one side of each pair to know the other's address. On a Synology, the side is forced. The Tailscale package runs in userspace mode: the NAS accepts connections from the tailnet, but can't open any. So every device holds the NAS address, and the NAS keeps every device as . Without discovery, means the NAS never dials anybody.

Then, create the folder. Click and choose the path on the NAS. Leave the tab empty for now. Devices come next, and they introduce themselves. In the tab, choose . The NAS keeps the last few versions of each file in a folder. It's the only device that does.

On macOS, Homebrew does the job:

brew install syncthing
brew services start syncthing

The web interface is at . Apply the same connection settings as on the NAS. Open on the NAS web interface, and on the laptop click . Paste the NAS identifier and set its address to tcp://nas.<tailnet>.ts.net:22000. Within a minute, the NAS shows a banner: a new device wants to connect.

Accept it, leave its address as , and tick the folder in the tab. The laptop then shows the folder offer. Accept it and set the path to where you want to store your files. When it works, the NAS lists the laptop as connected, and the folder reads "Up to Date" on both sides. At home, Tailscale connects the two directly on the LAN, so the same address works everywhere.

macOS refuses background processes access to Documents, Desktop, and Downloads unless you grant it explicitly. Syncthing runs as a background service, so a folder under Documents stops with "operation not permitted". Keep synced folders elsewhere, for example.

Syncthing has no official iOS client. I use Sync Anything. It's freemium: the free version synchronizes to one single folder on one single device. If you want more, you know what to do.

On the phone, add the NAS by scanning the QR code from the NAS's screen. Tap on the NAS entry and replace with tcp://nas.<tailnet>.ts.net:22000.

Accept the phone on the NAS and tick the folder, as for the laptop. Accept the folder on the phone. Sync Anything doesn't expose the connection switches, so the phone still announces itself to the discovery servers and may use a relay. With the NAS address set, it connects over Tailscale first. That's the leak I couldn't close.

One thing differs from the laptop: iOS doesn't allow apps to run permanently in the background. Sync happens while the app is open, and opportunistically otherwise. Note that Tailscale must be up on the phone too.

KeePassium and KeePassXC setup

Nothing changes on the laptop: KeePassXC opens the file from the synced folder. On the phone, open KeePassium, add a database, and browse the Files app to the Sync Anything location. KeePassium reads and writes a local file. No cloud connector, and no reason to re-add the database, so the security key stays in the drawer.

Syncthing shares folders, not a root. , , with . It's a great benefit compared to Dropbox and Google Drive, as they sync a single root folder, and the most you can do is pick which subfolders a device gets.

In practice, I don't use it yet. For now, I sync a single root folder with the NAS, which only contains the password database. Photos go through Synology Photos, which has its own app. Payslips are the next candidate, but I don't need them on my phone, and I seldom read them at all. That's a question of long-term storage rather than sync, and a design problem for another day.

The setup has trade-offs, however.

Four devices, no server, and a file written as a whole on every change: conflicts are possible. If I edit the database on the phone while offline, then on the laptop, Syncthing keeps both and renames one . KeePassXC can merge two databases, so recovery is a matter of minutes. It didn't happen to me yet, but I know I'm covered in case.

Because of the iOS background restriction, the phone copy can lag. I need to open Sync Anything before KeePassium when I know I changed a password. It's a habit, not a solution.

Also, the star topology means that when the NAS is down, nothing syncs. The laptop and phone each keep their last copy and carry on. It's acceptable for me, since the NAS is the most reliable device in the house. Pairing the laptop directly with the phone would remove the issue, but Sync Anything's free tier allows a single remote device.

Finally, I don't run a database backup. It exists on four devices, but four copies that stay identical aren't a backup: a deletion or a corrupted save would propagate to all four within seconds. That's why the NAS keeps old versions. It covers potentially bad edits. The NAS itself isn't backed up; if it dies, three current copies survive, but the history goes with it. I accept that. RAID 5 covers a dead disk, and the history is a convenience, not a necessity.

My password database forced me to question where my files live. The answer is on my machines, and only there. Syncthing does the synchronization, and Tailscale gives it a private network with stable names. I'm happy to move away from Google Drive, even if for one file.

Bit by bit, step by step. The next ones are files that I read often but don't write often, and archive files.

items.content: The FAA announced today that it is finally phasing out floppy disks from air traffic control systems at more than 400 facilities. The FAA plans to have E-IDS installed in 435 sites by the end of 2028; the first five locations to receive the upgrades are the Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport and Greater Rochester International Airport, as well as data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City.

items.title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch Is Changing the Color of the Ocean
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Scientific American: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, an area in the Pacific Ocean where debris naturally accumulates, is full of tiny bits of plastic -- so full, in fact, that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean. [...] To better understand how microplastics may have influenced the ocean's color, [Daniel Koestner, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Bergen in Norway] and his colleagues looked at 20 years of satellite data from the spot in the ocean with perhaps the most of plastic -- the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a zone between Hawaii and California where trash trapped by ocean currents accumulates.
 
Between 2002 and 2022, the researchers found, waters near the garbage patch have gotten brighter in both blue and green wavelengths compared with surrounding areas. The results, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on Thursday, don't yet prove that microplastics have directly brightened the ocean, the researchers emphasize, though their findings are backed up by lab experiments with microplastics. But without taking direct ocean samples, it's hard to know for sure what's causing the ocean's color to change.
"We're still one step away from proving definitively that microplastics are causing the shift in color that that we're seeing," adds study co-author Shea Cheatham, a Ph.D. student also at the University of Bergen. "We just have to get in there [to the garbage patch] to verify."
 
The hope is that detecting these color shifts could help identify other areas around the world where microplastics have accumulated.

items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Joe_Dragon shares a report from TechCrunch: Applebee's has fixed a security flaw that allowed anyone to access the personal information of its registered customers, after a researcher found a password for an internal database inside Applebee's mobile app, TechCrunch has learned. The popular restaurant chain confirmed [last Thursday] that it had taken action to address the security issue to prevent any unauthorized access to its customer database. [...] The exposed database contained customer names, email addresses (including whether or not the customer verified their email), dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes. The data also included veteran status, the number of times customers had logged in, when their accounts were created, and the IP addresses of their most recent log-ins, which can be used to reveal the person's approximate location.
 
[...] When asked by TechCrunch, the spokesperson would not say if the company has server logs that it can review to determine whether anyone accessed the database, or if it has any logs at all. "Our investigation is ongoing, and we will take appropriate steps based on our findings," the company added. It's unclear how many customers were affected by the data exposure. [...] Applebee's had at least 8.5 million customers enrolled in its rewards program as of last year, though the company would not provide a number of how many customers had their personal information exposed by this security flaw.

items.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.

The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

One connection, works every time, needs no retries

There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

items.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
"OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article: Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:
 
 - Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
 - Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We'll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
 - Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We'll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We'll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
 
[...] The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That's what we're committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

items.title: Small Tweaks, Great Output: What Merchants Can Do to Maximize Pay By Bank Conversion
items.author: Noda
items.content:
Open banking payments are a genuinely good deal for merchants. Lower transaction fees than cards, near-instant access to settled funds, no card chargeback headaches. But in many markets, it's still a relatively new checkout option, and even where the infrastructure is mature (think the UK, the Netherlands or Germany), plenty of shoppers still default to what they know – cards, PayPal or other methods. In Central and Eastern Europe, awareness is growing fast, but it's still an education curve.

So how do you nudge your users to pick it? There are two ways to get there.

Some solutions, like Noda’s , use smart routing through the card form to bring Pay by Bank into the payment flow without any changes to your checkout UI.

But if Pay by Bank is a visible option in your checkout, how it’s presented makes all the difference. We asked Lucy Oganisian, Product Designer at Noda, to share a few practical UX tweaks that can help merchants improve Pay by Bank conversion – whether you're running a WooCommerce store on a plugin that allows basic customisation or engineering a fully custom checkout from scratch.

Here's what actually works, tested and approved by our team.

1. Get the Button Name Right

Tests show that vague labels quietly kill conversion. Button names like leave users uncertain about what they're actually doing – and uncertain users don't convert.

 is becoming a recognizable standard in the same way  is. Moreover, when  and  sit next to each other, the choice feels obvious and balanced, not like one is the main event and the other is a footnote.

The same applies to localised checkouts: clear and direct translations tend to perform better than more creative alternatives.

When a payment method is unfamiliar, users look for anchors they already trust. Bank logos are one of the most powerful  you can add, and they cost nothing to display.

A small row of recognisable bank marks near your Pay by Bank option signals two things:  and . That second part matters a lot. Users want to know their specific institution is supported before they proceed further.

Some providers like Trustly or Klarna push their own branding at this touchpoint, but that tells users very little if they've never heard of them. Familiar bank marks work like trust badges but more credible – because they're institutions users already rely on.

Hiding the Pay by Bank option below the fold is a pain point that hits hardest on mobile. If users need to scroll to discover it, it becomes the "backup plan" option, not a first choice. And that's exactly how it'll convert.

A couple of things to avoid: placing it out of the visible area on load, and creating multiple equally prominent buttons on one screen. When users face two "main" actions, they hesitate.

As for where exactly to put it: in markets where Pay by Bank is already a well-known checkout option, don't hesitate to place it first. In markets where awareness is still building, second position works nicely – visible and clearly labelled but not demanding attention before the user is ready.

4. Don't Overwhelm With Options

Placing individual bank buttons directly into your checkout can be a great way to minimize further screens and potential drop-offs – especially for e-commerce flows.

But there's a ceiling. In many European markets, the top 3–5 banks cover roughly 70–90% of users, so short preview serves the majority without cluttering the experience. Showing, for example, 5 banks tends to outperform showing 9: decisions feel easier, the flow stays pleasant, and conversion follows. The rest can live behind a "show more" option – accessible, but out of the way.

5. Colors & Text – Keep Them Consistent

It’'s best to pick button colours that are consistent with your website. If the Pay by Bank button style clashes with your site's design – users notice, even if they can't articulate why.

The same goes for typography: text that fails to meet WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) requirements can easily become unreadable, often due to low contrast or font size. It excludes some users and signals a lack of polish to the rest.

If you're using a plugin and your provider offers customisation features, spend a few minutes on the appearance settings after setup. It's among the quickest, highest-return things you can do.

None of this requires significant technical investment. But these details do shape how Pay by Bank is perceived at checkout. Pay by Bank is often viewed as an attractive option for merchants. A few thoughtful tweaks can make it the more obvious choice for their customers too. What often determines uptake is how naturally the option appears in the user journey. When Pay by Bank feels visible, trustworthy and well-integrated, customers are far more likely to choose it.

items.title: OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports: Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
 
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins. The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit. This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
 
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes. [...] Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH. Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.

items.title: How Crypto Wallets Are Becoming More Than Just Wallets
items.author: Obyte
items.content:
At the beginning of Bitcoin, there was no such thing as a crypto wallet as we know it today. You had a full node, took care of complex private keys, and that was it. A lot has changed since then. Simpler and lighter apps appeared over the years, making it easier for users to manage their coins. But the evolution didn’t end there: now, crypto wallets are more than just wallets.

These versatile apps can do a lot of things beyond just storing funds, signing transactions, and sending payments. Of course, it always depends on the brand and network(s) involved, but we can find many interesting features to take advantage of in numerous crypto wallets. Let’s explore some of them.

Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI)

Historically, people's "identity"—even in the digital realm—has always been assigned and managed by third parties (governments, corporations, etc.). However, the decentralized world offers an alternative through the (SSI) model. As the name implies, this is a form of identity or personal verification that can only be managed by the user who owns that identity.

In this way, very specific data can be shared only when necessary, rather than all personal information—for example, only age is verified, and the name is never revealed. Some crypto wallets can handle this type of digital ID already, in different ways. In an SSI setup, the wallet generally stores the credential and its cryptographic keys on the user's device. The issuer creates and signs the credential, while a decentralized network may store a DID (decentralized identifier), public key, credential schema, or revocation/status information that helps verify it.

When the user presents the credential, the recipient checks the issuer's signature and relevant on-chain data without needing the credential itself to be public. Examples of wallets that already have this feature include Dock Wallet, cheqd Wallet, Privado ID Wallet, and the . In the latter, you can verify your real name, your email, your GitHub account, your status as an accredited investor by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and more.

All of this is done via chatbots integrated into the same wallet. Then, the information is stored in your wallet, and you can selectively share parts of that information with whoever you like.

Chats, Messages, & Chatbots

You can't communicate directly with your transaction peers in every crypto wallet, but you can in some of them—and with end-to-end encryption, too. You can even send messages on-chain, if you want, and enjoy some easier chatbots here and there. Depending on the system, messages may travel through a peer-to-peer network and be read only by the intended recipient, and never by someone else.

As for more public that will last forever, this can be done even on Bitcoin, but it’s not exactly user-friendly there. The process often involves converting your message to hexadecimal code, finding specific wallets that support this function or advanced features inside wallets, and pasting that hex code into a designated field, sending a transaction without funds. In other crypto networks and wallets, it’s just a matter of writing whatever you want in a user-friendly menu, pressing “send,” and paying a small transaction fee.

aren’t that common, but they can be welcome, especially for beginners. They can respond to commands or help users perform actions from a familiar chat interface. They can be related to Large-Language Models (LLMs) like or , or simply follow ingrained instructions without the risks associated with AI, like the Obyte Wallet. In the latter one, you can enjoy all of these features: encrypted chat, user-friendly on-chain messages, and classic chatbots.

Programmable Transactions & Smart Contracts

These days, it’s rare that your crypto wallet can’t interact with smart contracts and make programmable transactions. Smart contracts are small computer programs stored in a certain ledger and designed to carry out specific, pre-set rules. They can automate payments, exchanges, loans, bets, games, and many other applications.

In practice, when you’re inside a crypto wallet, the most you will typically see regarding a smart contract is by a specific Dapp to connect to your address and, likely, use some of your funds. Unless you are a developer, you probably have little idea how to "read" one—let alone create one. Most wallets won’t show you this, either, but there are some of them with friendlier smart contracts.

Besides, if you’re sending a transaction or interacting with a Dapp, you’ll be able to see a clear preview of the results and fees before pressing “Send” or “Pay.”

Remember the familiar routine of creating a new account for every website? Wallet-based authentication offers another route. With Sign-In with Ethereum (SIWE), for instance, a user can prove control of an account by signing a message. The signature happens inside the wallet, while the application verifies it. The standard was designed to give Ethereum accounts a consistent way to authenticate with services outside the network itself.

This can make one on-chain account useful across multiple applications. The address acts as a persistent identity that can be used across many Dapps, with the wallet handling the signature needed to prove control. Beyond for Ethereum, other providers of this feature include and for multiple networks.

There’s also an important privacy detail here: signing in doesn’t automatically reveal a person’s legal name, address, or other real-world information. What an application receives depends on the authentication system and the information the user chooses to provide.

Beyond your own businesses, you can also contribute to your community and help shape the future of your favorite networks by participating in governance. lets token holders vote on proposals whose results can trigger changes to a network’s rules, parameters, treasury, or other functions. The voting process and its powers vary from one network to another, but the wallet can provide the place where users review proposals, connect their address, and cast a vote with their governance tokens.

The mechanics can be quite simple. A proposal appears in a governance interface, the wallet shows the vote and any required transaction, and the user confirms it by signing. Some systems use delegated voting, so users can assign their voting power to another address instead. In other cases, holding a specific token or meeting a balance requirement determines who can participate.

Examples include MetaMask supporting governance voting through compatible Dapps, Keplr providing governance features for Cosmos networks, and Obyte allowing users to participate in on-chain voting through its wallet and .

In the end, the word “wallet” is starting to sound a little undersized for all of this. The same account can connect a person to applications, support communication, authenticate access, interact with programmable software, and even decide on the future of a network. A crypto wallet remains a place to manage digital assets, but its role can extend much further, and it'll likely continue to do so.

items.title: Gate Pioneers Proof of Security, Achieving 104.58% Cold Storage Coverage to Solidify Asset Security
items.author: Blockman PR and Marketing
items.content:
Gate has officially introduced Proof of Security (PoSEC), a new asset security verification framework, becoming the first digital asset trading platform in the industry to launch a PoSEC security verification system. Since its founding in 2013, Gate has consistently placed user asset security at the forefront of its priorities.

With the introduction of PoSEC, Gate extends security verification beyond reserve adequacy to include asset storage structures and risk coverage capabilities, further solidifying safeguards for user assets and providing a new practical approach to advancing industry security standards.

PoSEC Focuses on Asset Storage Security and Quantifies Extreme-Risk Coverage Capabilities

Unlike Proof of Reserves (PoR), which primarily verifies the adequacy of asset reserves, PoSEC places additional emphasis on asset storage security. By publicly disclosing the distribution of assets between platform cold storage and hot wallets, PoSEC provides visibility into asset storage structures and their ability to cover potential losses under extreme scenarios.

PoSEC introduces the cold storage coverage ratio as a key metric to measure the extent to which cold storage covers total user assets. A coverage ratio ≥ 100% means that, under the applicable calculation methodology, cold storage alone would be sufficient to cover all user assets even if all assets held in hot wallets were lost. PoR and PoSEC serve complementary purposes, extending asset security verification from reserve adequacy to storage security and risk coverage, while providing users with more comprehensive and transparent information about asset security.

Cold Storage Coverage Reaches 104.58%, with Open and Transparent Storage Structure

According to the snapshot taken at 00:00 (UTC) on November 4, 2026, Gate's cold storage coverage ratio reached 104.58%, with cold storage and hot wallet assets accounting for 88.26% and 11.74% of total assets, respectively. Cold storage assets include digital assets held offline and traditional assets under independent custody. To qualify, these assets must meet requirements such as not being directly used for routine deposits and withdrawals, being held offline or under independent custody, requiring multi-party authorization for transfers, and being independently verifiable.

The current data is undergoing verification by an independent third-party audit firm. The review covers asset authenticity and control, valuation and calculation methodologies, and coverage ratio calculations. The audit report will be published on Gate's official website upon completion, enhancing the transparency and credibility of asset security disclosures.

From PoR to PoSEC: Continuously Strengthening Digital Asset Security

Gate has long been committed to digital asset security and transparency. In 2020, Gate was among the first in the industry to introduce an open-source Proof of Reserves (PoR) mechanism and a Merkle Tree-based asset verification solution, establishing itself as an early contributor to reserve transparency in the industry. Gate subsequently incorporated technologies such as zk-SNARKs to enhance its asset reserve verification framework.

As of October 18, 2026, Gate's total reserves amounted to approximately $8.688 billion, with an overall reserve ratio of 118.49%. The platform also employs a range of security mechanisms, including hot and cold wallet segregation, multi-signature technology, Multi-Party Computation (MPC), dynamic risk monitoring, and zero-trust access control, to establish a multi-layered security framework covering asset reserves, storage management, and risk protection.

From PoR, which verifies reserve adequacy, to PoSEC, which verifies asset storage security and risk coverage capabilities, Gate is progressively building a multi-layered security framework encompassing asset reserves, storage management, risk protection, and public verification. Looking ahead, Gate will continue to uphold its security-first principle, further develop PoSEC standards and verification mechanisms, and collaborate with more industry participants to enhance asset security and transparency, laying a stronger security foundation for the long-term, sustainable development of the digital asset industry.

Learn more:

Gate, founded in 2013 by Dr. Han, is one of the world's leading cryptocurrency and integrated financial services platforms, spanning financial and everyday use cases including asset management, trading and payments. Serving over 62 million users globally, it supports trading across 5,400+ digital assets and 12,800+ stock assets and ETFs, while providing access to a comprehensive range of TradFi assets, including metals, stocks, indices, forex, and commodities to meet users' end-to-end needs across asset holding, trading, and spending. As an industry benchmark, Gate was among the first platforms to implement 100% Proof of Reserves. items.title: OpenMatter Network Positions Decentralized Computing as an Alternative To Data Centers for AI
items.author: CyberNewswire
items.content:
Melbourne, Florida, November 5th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--, a pioneer in decentralized infrastructure for agentic artificial intelligence, is positioning its decentralized computing platform as an alternative to massive, centralized data center development amid growing public opposition to new facilities.

The company says its approach can support continued AI adoption by enabling computing workloads to run across distributed resources rather than relying primarily on large-scale data center infrastructure.

The results of Tuesday's midterm elections have put growing public opposition to massive data center development in the national spotlight. However, according to OpenMatter Network, resistance to new facilities need not signal a slowdown in AI adoption. Instead, it could accelerate the transition to a computing model that reduces dependence on massive, centralized data centers.

“Voters have made it clear that they are increasingly concerned about the enormous energy demands, environmental impact and rising utility costs associated with massive data center development,” said Mike Anderson, CEO of OpenMatter Network. “But the need to deploy agentic AI isn’t going away. Businesses don’t have to choose between advancing AI and addressing these very legitimate concerns. There is another path forward, and OpenMatter is helping make it possible.”

Across the country, communities have expressed concerns about the impact of large-scale facilities on electricity rates, water supplies, local infrastructure and the environment. The election has brought renewed attention to those concerns and the policy choices surrounding new construction.

“The assumption that AI must be built around increasingly massive concentrations of computing power deserves to be challenged,” Anderson continued. “Our decentralized architecture allows computing resources to be distributed across many different locations. That means organizations have another way to move forward with agentic AI as communities and policymakers reconsider the costs and consequences of building more enormous data centers.”

The OpenMatter Network platform is designed to transform widely available computing hardware into usable network resources through its distributed architecture, algorithms and verifiable computing capabilities. By enabling independently owned computing resources to participate in a shared network, OpenMatter is working to make decentralized infrastructure a practical alternative for enterprise AI deployment.

“There’s an enormous amount of computing capacity outside the walls of traditional data centers,” said Renee Davis, co-founder and chief business officer of OpenMatter Network. “Our technology makes it possible to bring those resources together in a verifiable network capable of supporting real-world AI workloads. Rather than concentrating computing power in a relatively small number of massive facilities, we can distribute workloads across existing resources and smaller installations, creating opportunities for a more flexible and potentially more energy-efficient approach to AI infrastructure.”

The decentralized model also offers organizations greater flexibility in where computing resources are located and how they are deployed. This can be particularly valuable for businesses and government institutions seeking greater control over computing infrastructure, including those with requirements for data sovereignty and locally managed resources.

“The question is no longer simply how many more massive data centers we need to build,” Anderson concluded. “It’s how we can deploy the AI capabilities businesses need without imposing unnecessary burdens on the communities where computing resources are located. Tuesday’s election results make that question more urgent than ever. OpenMatter offers a new way forward.”

Headquartered in Florida’s Space Coast, is building the Verifiable Trust Layer for Secure Collaboration and AI Agents. Guided by the principle “Don’t Trust Data. Prove It.,” the company’s cryptographically verifiable architecture enables secure collaboration, governed AI behavior and mathematically verifiable execution across untrusted environments. For more information, visit .

items.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader bbsguru shares a report from KrebsOnSecurity: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
 
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into "free" mobile and desktop applications. Infatica's founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia's state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. [...] Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight. Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network. "This is public access," the Layer3 Intel team wrote. "Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services."

items.title: Building Data Observability for Banking Pipelines
items.author: Sunilkumar Reddy Eraganeni
items.content:
Loud failures are easy. A job crashes, the scheduler turns red, somebody gets paged, and within the hour there is a chat thread with far too many people in it. Annoying, sure, but the system is at least telling you the truth.

The failure I worry about is the quiet one. Every task shows green. The report lands on time. And one number inside it is wrong, because a feed stopped refreshing three days ago or a join started dropping rows, and nothing in the stack was built to care.

In most industries that is an embarrassing dashboard. In banking it can turn into a regulatory submission, a liquidity figure in front of a risk committee, or a customer statement. The stakes shift quite a lot. So this piece is about silent failures: what they look like, why banks are unusually exposed to them, and a way of building observability that catches them before a report breaks. I should say early that it will not catch everything. I'll come back to what it misses.

Why banking data fails quietly

I can think of three reasons, though there are probably more.

First, the chains are long. A single regulatory figure, say a liquidity coverage ratio, might pass through a core banking extract, a treasury system, a reference data service, a staging layer, a transformation layer and finally a reporting tool. Each hop belongs to someone else, often with a release calendar nobody downstream has seen.

Second, banks lean heavily on batch. Plenty of critical feeds arrive once a day, and some only once a month. If a daily feed breaks on Tuesday, you might not see the damage until the Friday reconciliation, or the month-end close. A long feedback loop gives bad data plenty of time to travel.

Third, and this is the uncomfortable one, a lot of existing monitoring answers the question "did the job run?" when the question that matters is "is the data right?" Those are different questions. A job can run perfectly and load nothing at all.

What a silent failure looks like

None of the following is a real incident from a named bank, but the shapes are familiar to anyone who has worked near a data warehouse.

An FX rates feed from a market data vendor stops updating after a change on the vendor side. Your pipeline keeps reading the table, which still has plenty of rows, so the job-level check passes. Euro and dollar positions get converted at last Wednesday's rate. Totals look sensible. They just are not true.

An upstream team changes a code in a product reference table, perhaps a new product type with no mapping yet. An inner join quietly drops everything that no longer matches. Three percent of the loan book disappears from a report. Three percent does not look dramatic on a chart. In a capital calculation, it might be very dramatic.

The drifting distribution. A source system starts defaulting a null field, like days past due, to zero. Row counts are identical. The schema is identical. But the share of loans classed as current jumps overnight, and nobody changed a credit policy.

None of these throws an exception. All of them pass a "job succeeded" check.

Monitoring is not observability (roughly)

I'm a bit wary of the word "observability" because vendors have stretched it until it covers almost anything. The distinction I find useful is simple. Monitoring checks things you already know can go wrong. Observability means collecting enough information about the data itself, continuously, that when something strange happens you can work out where it started and what it touched.

For data, that mostly means watching the data and not only the machinery. CPU on the warehouse tells you very little about whether the FX table is current.

Five signals worth tracking

There are lots of ways to slice this. The five below are the ones I keep coming back to, partly because each maps neatly to one of the failures above.

When did this table last change, compared with when it should have? One trap here: check the business date inside the data, not the load timestamp. A job can load yesterday's rates today and look perfectly fresh by the wrong clock. That is exactly how the stale rate table slips through.

Are row counts in a plausible range? The word that matters is plausible, because banks have calendars. UK bank holidays, month-end, quarter-end and year-end all change expected volumes. A check that ignores them will cry wolf every few weeks, and people will stop listening.

Have columns been added, dropped or retyped? This is the cheapest signal to collect and often the most useful, since a renamed column is a common cause of everything downstream going subtly wrong.

Null rates, value ranges, category proportions, and sums of balances. This is where the drifting distribution gets caught. It is also the noisiest signal, so I would introduce it last.

Which reports depend on this table? When a check fails, lineage tells you the blast radius. Without it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging" and everyone shrugs. With it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging, and it feeds the liquidity report due at 10am". That is a very different conversation.

Here is the layout I would sketch on a whiteboard. The main idea is that checks live at the boundaries between layers, not only at the end next to the report.

Reading it left to right, the data moves from source systems through ingestion, raw storage, staging, curated marts, and finally the regulatory and management reports. Underneath, an observability layer attaches a different kind of check to each stage.

At ingestion, you ask the cheap questions: did the file arrive, is it fresh by business date, does the schema match the agreed contract? In staging, you look at keys, referential integrity and null rates. In the marts, you run reconciliations and distribution checks. At the report layer, you compare control totals against the prior period and against the general ledger.

Reconciliation deserves a special mention because it is old-fashioned and brilliant. Finance teams have done it for decades. The idea is that the sum of balances in your mart should equal the sum in the source extract, within a tolerance. If a join drops three percent of the loan book, a control total notices immediately, even though row counts and schemas look fine. Plenty of data teams skip it because it feels unglamorous. I would start there.

Every check writes its result to a metadata store. That store feeds the alerting layer and, ideally, a lineage graph, so a failure can be traced to the reports it threatens.

A small example of the volume check, written as plain SQL so it is easy to port. It compares the latest day against the same weekday over the past eight weeks. Treat it as a sketch rather than production code, because it knows nothing about holidays yet.

WITH history AS (
  SELECT business_date, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM staging.loan_positions
  WHERE business_date >= :run_date - INTERVAL '56 days'
    AND business_date <  :run_date
    AND EXTRACT(DOW FROM business_date) = EXTRACT(DOW FROM :run_date)
  GROUP BY business_date
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT AVG(n) AS avg_n, STDDEV(n) AS sd_n FROM history
),
latest AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM staging.loan_positions
  WHERE business_date = :run_date
)
SELECT latest.n,
       baseline.avg_n,
       ABS(latest.n - baseline.avg_n) / NULLIF(baseline.sd_n, 0) AS z_score
FROM latest, baseline;

If the z-score goes past something like 3, raise a flag. The threshold is a guess you will tune, and you should expect to be wrong about it the first few times.

Alerts people will not ignore

Collecting signals is the easy half. The harder half is making sure a human reacts to them.

I have seen, or at least heard enough war stories to believe in, the pattern where a team switches on two hundred checks, gets forty alerts a day, and within a month has muted the channel. At that point you have built an expensive way of generating noise. So the design question is less "what can we check?" and more "what deserves to interrupt someone?"

A scheme that tends to hold up has three tiers. Informational checks get logged and reviewed weekly. Warnings go to the named owner of the dataset during working hours. Critical failures, meaning anything that touches a regulatory report, go to the owner immediately and also close a gate in front of the publish step.

That gate is the controversial part. Some teams prefer to publish anyway with a visible warning banner, on the argument that a late report is worse than a flagged one. Others hold the previous approved version until someone signs off. I lean towards holding for regulatory outputs and warning for internal dashboards, but I can see the other side. If your submission deadline is fixed by a regulator, the calculation changes.

Whichever way you go, two things matter more than the tooling. Every dataset needs a named owner, a person and not a shared inbox. And upstream teams need a lightweight data contract, even a one-page agreement, saying which columns and codes they promise not to change without notice. Without that, you are monitoring someone else's decisions with no way to influence them.

I would be overselling it if I stopped there.

Observability catches data that is stale, missing, malformed or oddly distributed. It does not catch data that is fresh, complete, consistent and simply wrong because the business logic misreads a rule. A risk weight applied to the wrong asset class will sail through every check described above. That needs code review, testing and domain experts, and no dashboard replaces them.

Thresholds can also create false confidence. A check tuned so loosely that it never fires is worse than no check, because people assume it is protecting them. Anomaly detection tools driven by machine learning can help with tuning, but I am slightly cautious about them in a regulated setting. An auditor can read a rule that says "volume within three standard deviations of the weekday baseline". A black box that quietly adapts its own thresholds is harder to defend.

And then there is the organisational side, which no architecture diagram captures. If upstream teams see your alerts as an accusation and not a courtesy, the checks will be ignored. A bit of diplomacy goes a long way here.

If I were starting on Monday, I would not try to cover the whole warehouse. I would pick one regulatory report, trace its lineage back to the ten or so tables it truly depends on, and add three things: freshness by business date, a volume check with a calendar, and a control total that reconciles to source.

Then I would assign owners and run everything in warn-only mode for two weeks. That gives you a feel for false positives before anyone is woken up at night. Only after that would I switch the critical checks to blocking.

That staged approach is slower than a big-bang rollout, and some teams will find it frustrating. But it builds trust in the alerts, and trust is the thing that decides whether anyone responds when the real one fires.

Silent failures are hard because they look like success. The pipeline is green, the report is on time, and the number is wrong. Catching them means shifting attention from whether the job ran to whether the data still makes sense, and doing it at every boundary, not just at the finish line.

None of this is exotic. Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage, plus a few reconciliations that finance has trusted for decades. The hard parts are the unglamorous ones: ownership, contracts, tuning thresholds and keeping the noise low enough that people still care. If your team is working through the same problem, I would be curious which of the five signals you found most useful in practice. My bet is freshness by business date, but I could easily be wrong.

items.title: Debugging macOS LaunchAgent Failures With launchctl and Exit Code 78
items.author: Malek Damiri
items.content:
Every morning at 7:45, a job on my Mac runs a reconciliation and posts the results for the finance team. It's an ordinary LaunchAgent: a plist in , a Python script, and a log file.

For three mornings in October, it didn't run.

Nothing told me. There was no error in Slack, because the code that sends errors never started. There was no crash report. And the log file, the first place anyone looks, had nothing new in it, because the job failed before it could write a line.

The only clue was a number.

launchd keeps a record of every job's last exit. Ask for it:

launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.example.cash-recon | grep -E "runs|last exit code"

	runs = 1
	last exit code = 78: EX_CONFIG

The labels in this post are examples. For a quick look at every job, shows the last exit status in its second column.

78 is from , a configuration error. My script never exits with 78, and that's the tell: when the exit code is one your program doesn't use, your program probably never ran.

What 78 means for a LaunchAgent

Before launchd starts your program, it does some setup. It opens the files named in and , changes into , and finds the executable. If any of that fails, your program never starts, and the job ends with 78.

I wanted to know exactly which mistakes produce it, so I loaded a set of deliberately broken test jobs on macOS 26.6 and read what launchd reported:

what was wrong                                 last exit code
program path doesn't exist                     78: EX_CONFIG
WorkingDirectory doesn't exist                 78: EX_CONFIG
log file in a folder launchd can't write to    78: EX_CONFIG
log folder doesn't exist                       0   (launchd creates it)
nothing; the program ran and failed            1   (the program's own code)

Two things surprised me. launchd happily creates a missing log folder, so that's not your problem. And a log file it can't open is fatal. Not a warning and not a quiet fallback: the whole job stops, and the error has nowhere to go.

My job's logs pointed at a folder on the Desktop, next to the script. The Desktop is one of the folders that macOS privacy protection (TCC) guards, along with Documents, Downloads, iCloud Drive, and removable and network volumes. When launchd isn't allowed to open a log file there, you get the same 78 as any other path it can't write to.

Moving the logs to , which privacy protection doesn't guard, fixed it that morning. The script and its working directory still live on the Desktop and run fine. Only the files launchd opens itself had to move.

One honest caveat. When I later tried to reproduce the Desktop failure on purpose, a test job I loaded from a terminal wrote to the Desktop without complaint. Privacy decisions depend on context, including which process is asking and what it has been granted, so the same plist can behave differently depending on how and when it was loaded. A folder without write permission reproduces exit 78 every time. The Desktop didn't. That inconsistency is exactly why I stopped putting anything launchd opens in a protected folder. "Works when I test it" is not the same as "works at 7:45 when nobody's watching."

Test the fix without waiting until tomorrow

The worst part of debugging a 7:45 job is the 23-hour feedback loop. You don't need it. Copy the plist, give it a new label, swap the program for something harmless, and tell it to run at load. Everything launchd sets up stays the same, so if the setup is broken, you'll see 78 in two seconds:

plutil -convert xml1 -o /tmp/test.plist ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.cash-recon.plist
plutil -replace Label -string com.example.cash-recon.test /tmp/test.plist
plutil -replace ProgramArguments -json '["/usr/bin/true"]' /tmp/test.plist
plutil -replace RunAtLoad -bool true /tmp/test.plist

launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) /tmp/test.plist
sleep 2
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.example.cash-recon.test | grep "last exit code"
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.example.cash-recon.test

does nothing and exits 0. If the copy still reports 78, the problem is in the setup, not your code. Fix the plist, rerun the copy, and only then touch the real job. Reload the real one with and so launchd reads the new version.

A doctor for every LaunchAgent

Once I'd found one of these, I wanted to check the rest. This script reads every plist in , flags the setups that end in 78, and prints each job's last exit code:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check every LaunchAgent for the problems that end in exit code 78 (EX_CONFIG).

Usage: python3 launchd_doctor.py [folder]   (default: ~/Library/LaunchAgents)
"""
import os
import plistlib
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HOME = Path.home()
# Folders macOS privacy protection (TCC) guards. launchd may not be allowed to open files here.
PROTECTED = [HOME / "Desktop", HOME / "Documents", HOME / "Downloads",
             HOME / "Library" / "Mobile Documents", Path("/Volumes")]


def short(path):
    return str(path).replace(str(HOME), "~", 1)


def last_exit(label):
    out = subprocess.run(["launchctl", "print", f"gui/{os.getuid()}/{label}"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    m = re.search(r"last exit code = (.+)", out)
    return m.group(1).strip() if m else ("never exited" if out else "not loaded")


def problems(job):
    found = []
    args = job.get("ProgramArguments") or [job.get("Program", "")]
    program = job.get("Program") or args[0]
    if not Path(program).exists():
        found.append(f"program not found: {short(program)}")
    workdir = job.get("WorkingDirectory")
    if workdir and not Path(workdir).is_dir():
        found.append(f"working directory not found: {short(workdir)}")
    for key in ("StandardOutPath", "StandardErrorPath"):
        log = job.get(key)
        if log and any(Path(log).is_relative_to(p) for p in PROTECTED):
            found.append(f"{key} is in a protected folder: {short(log)}")
    return found


def main():
    folder = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else HOME / "Library" / "LaunchAgents"
    for plist in sorted(folder.glob("*.plist")):
        with plist.open("rb") as f:
            job = plistlib.load(f)
        label = job.get("Label", plist.stem)
        status, issues = last_exit(label), problems(job)
        flag = "!!" if issues or status.startswith("78") else "ok"
        print(f"{flag}  {label}  (last exit: {status})")
        for issue in issues:
            print(f"      - {issue}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run against a folder of example jobs:

!!  com.example.cash-recon  (last exit: not loaded)
      - StandardOutPath is in a protected folder: ~/Desktop/recon/cash-recon.log
      - StandardErrorPath is in a protected folder: ~/Desktop/recon/cash-recon.log
!!  com.example.crm-sync  (last exit: 78: EX_CONFIG)
      - program not found: /usr/local/bin/python3.11
ok  com.example.morning-report  (last exit: 0)
!!  com.example.weekly-export  (last exit: 78: EX_CONFIG)
      - working directory not found: ~/jobs/old-reports

is the classic upgrade casualty: Python moved, and the plist still points at the old interpreter. is a renamed folder. Both fail silently in exactly the same way mine did, and gets flagged before it ever has the chance.

The real lesson: watch for silence

The fix took five minutes. Noticing took three days, because every alert I had lived inside the job, and the job never ran. A job that doesn't start can't report its own failure.

What would have caught it on the first morning is a check that doesn't depend on the job at all: something separate that looks for the job's last success and complains when it's missing. It's the same principle I wrote about in small pipelines fail quietly: watch for the last success, not the last error.

The short version, for every LaunchAgent you rely on:

  • Logs go in . Nothing launchd opens lives in Desktop, Documents, Downloads, or iCloud Drive.
  • Use an absolute path to the interpreter, and recheck it after every Homebrew or Python upgrade.
  • Test plist changes with a run-at-load copy, not by waiting for the schedule.
  • Something other than the job watches for the job's success.
